ways.name: Downey Creek and the southern Ptarmigan corridor
ways.season: July to September, once the bushwhacking is out of snow and the glaciers are travellable.
ways.notes: The long way in from the west. Start at the Downey Creek trailhead off the Suiattle River Road and work through the southern end of the Ptarmigan Traverse corridor — Itswoot Ridge, Cub Lake and Bachelor Creek — on rugged, largely off-trail ground with real bushwhacking and glacier travel. Budget a full day, often two, before you are anywhere near rock. This is an experienced-mountaineers approach and nothing about it is a walk-in.

ways.name: Agnes Creek from the east
ways.season: July to September.
ways.notes: The other documented way into this range comes from the east, via the lake ferry and the long trail up Agnes Creek before leaving it for the brush. Parties using it camp on rock ridges above the glacier below the peaks rather than pushing on the same day. It is not a shortcut — the bushwhack off the trail takes most of a day on its own — but it puts you on the glacier side of the crest, which is the side this route starts from.

ways.name: Up the Cascade-Johannesburg Couloir to the C-J col
ways.season: May-Jun for continuous snow in the couloir
ways.notes:
The East Ridge is reached from the Cascade-Johannesburg col, and the direct way there is to climb the couloir that names it. The start is the Cascade Pass trailhead at about 3,600 ft: walk back down the road, drop the embankment into the valley, cross the Cascade River, and go over the moraine onto the couloir apron at roughly 3,300 ft — about twenty minutes from leaving the road. Then roughly 3,400 ft of booting to the col.

This is the fast way and the dangerous way. The couloir carries rock and ice fall from the Sill hanging glacier above, and the snow goes discontinuous where it narrows as the season progresses, so it is an early-season proposition.

The East Ridge by way of the C-J Couloir was first climbed in 1938 and is the most-used line on the peak; it and the other routes finishing on the south side are mostly scrambling.

ways.name: Cascade Pass, Mixup Arm and the Cache Glacier
ways.season: Jul-Sep
ways.notes:
The walking way in, avoiding the couloir entirely. Follow the Cascade Pass Trail from the trailhead at 3,600 ft for 3.5-3.7 miles and about 1,800 ft to Cascade Pass at roughly 5,400 ft. At the pass, near the benches, turn right and pick up the obvious climbers' path onto Mixup Arm.

Cross Mixup Arm and traverse and descend rightward until you reach the Cache Glacier — the described landmark is a seasonal waterfall, past which you turn right and ascend the lobe of the Cache.

One party using this side reported a long sidehill traverse beneath the Triplets and Cascade Peak, camping in a meadow below the C-J col at about 6,200 ft. That camp puts you at the base of the East Ridge for the following morning without ever entering the couloir.

Early season the traverse across Mixup's flank is snow-covered with a poor runout; late season Cache Col and the glacier edges can moat out.

ways.name: PCT from Snoqualmie Pass, leaving the trail half a mile short of Chikamin Pass
ways.season: July to September
ways.notes:
From the PCT North trailhead, Trail #2000, off I-90 exit 52, the trail switchbacks through timber and avalanche paths, crosses beneath Kendall Peak, and reaches the Kendall Katwalk around mile 5 at about 5,400 ft — a good checkpoint, though not reliable water late in the season.

Continue north past Ridge Lake at about mile 6.5, which has reliable camping and water, and the Alaska Lake and Joe Lake junctions, then along the rolling rocky PCT beneath Alaska and Huckleberry Mountains to the Huckleberry-Chikamin saddle around mile 10.25. The trail then contours below the Four Brothers and Chikamin's south face, passing the Park Lakes Trail junction.

About 13.5 miles one way to the base of the gullies with roughly 4,600 ft of gain, so most parties camp at Ridge Lake or the pack camp near the turnoff and make it a two or three day trip.

ways.name: Mineral Creek and Park Lakes, then the gullies above Glacier Lake
ways.season: July to September
ways.notes:
From the Mineral Creek trailhead, Trail #1331, at the end of FR-46 / Cooper Pass Road at about 2,400 ft, the trail is brushy low down but well trodden. It climbs steadily beside Mineral Creek to Park Lakes at 4.3 to 5.4 miles and about 2,570 ft of gain, and ties into the PCT.

From the PCT / Park Lakes junction, head north toward the Spectacle Point saddle overlooking Spectacle Lake, then drop about a mile to Glacier Lake, a common camp, before climbing the southeast-slope gullies above it.

This is the shortest line in — day-trip feasible for a strong party at roughly 14 to 16.5 miles round trip — but the tread is rougher and there are creek crossings low down.

ways.name: Lake outlet climbers' path into the west cirque
ways.season: mid-Jul-Sep, once the gully and cirque talus are snow-free
ways.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail #1599 for about 2.25 miles with a log-bridge crossing of Mountaineer Creek near the 1.5-mile mark, then left onto the Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A, a second log crossing, and steep rocky switchbacks to Colchuck Lake — about four miles and 2,280 ft, an hour and three quarters to two hours for a fit party carrying a rack.

The shorter of the two ways into the west cirque starts at the lake outlet, at the north end below the small dam. Cross there and follow a well-cairned climbers' path across the timbered hillside; it gains height quickly and deposits you on the talus field under the west face. Reckon about an hour from the lake, plus twenty to twenty-five minutes of boulder-hopping to reach the wall itself.

This is the way parties who have been there recommend, and it is the one to take unless the outlet crossing is unreasonable.

Colchuck Lake is the last water. The cirque and the route are dry.

ways.name: Southern line via the Aasgard-side slopes and the leftmost gully
ways.season: mid-Jul-Sep; the gully holds snow into early summer
ways.notes:
The alternative when you do not want to cross the outlet. Follow the lakeshore climbers' path counter-clockwise toward the slopes below Aasgard Pass, then cut north through a band of slide alder — look for cairns, because this is a genuine bushwhack — and climb the leftmost gully about 1,000 ft to its top. From there contour east on easy ground into the cirque.

An hour and a half to two hours from the lake, more gain than the outlet line and a lot more brush, but no ford. A winter/spring variation on the same idea follows a steepening gully starting near the lake's southwest edge.

In a heavy year the gully holds snow well into early summer and an axe or light traction is worth having.

name: Standard Route (Southeast Ridge via Jackita Ridge / Crater Lake Trail)

ways.name: Canyon Creek trailhead, Jackita Ridge #738 and the Crater Lake trail #746
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Oct; the Canyon Creek ford is the constraint in spring and early summer
ways.notes: Park at the Canyon Creek trailhead at about 1,900 ft on Highway 20 near milepost 141, roughly fifty-five miles west of Winthrop or thirty-three east of Marblemount. Vault toilet, no drinking water. There is no bridge over Canyon Creek on Jackita Ridge trail #738, and the Forest Service describes the crossing as difficult and potentially hazardous in spring and early summer. How people get across changes from year to year — one season a shin-deep wade a hundred yards upstream, another a log fifty metres up — so do not plan on a fixed method. The first mile and a half is brushy. The trail then climbs steeply through timber on a long series of switchbacks to the junction with the Crater Lake trail #746. That junction is unsigned, reported by two separate parties, and its elevation is published as either 5,000 or 5,260 ft. Turn onto #746 and climb toward Crater Lake. There is a second unmarked junction just before the lake, leading to the old east lookout site; stay with the main path, which runs along the south shore. Crater Lake is the last water — the ground above is dry, and the lake itself is shallow enough that water filtered at the outlet comes out warm. The whole peak is commonly given as fourteen to fifteen miles round trip with about 6,300 ft of gain.

ways.name: Devils Dome loop from the East Bank trailhead
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, as a multi-day trip
ways.notes:
A genuinely different approach with a specific purpose: it exists to avoid the Canyon Creek ford. The party who wrote it up said so directly, having judged a day trip from Canyon Creek to involve a difficult crossing at the time they were there.

It starts from the East Bank trailhead near Ruby Creek and runs roughly forty-eight miles with about 13,100 ft of gain over three days, taking in Devils Dome. That is a very different undertaking from the day-trip standard, and it is chosen for access rather than for the mountain.

Nothing is published on a Granite Creek or East Creek approach, so do not assume one exists.

ways.name: The Kindy Creek roadbed and the ribbon-marked climbers' trail to the Point 5116 saddle
ways.season: June through September
ways.notes:
From Marblemount, drive the river road about fourteen miles to the signed forest road 1570 junction and turn right. Cross the river on a concrete bridge and continue about half a mile to a Y-junction where the right fork is blocked by boulders; park there, at roughly 1,150 to 1,300 ft, because a long-standing washout keeps most parties from driving higher.

A climbers' trail flagged with pink ribbon every fifty to a hundred and fifty feet leaves the old roadbed and climbs steeply and directly through old growth - about seventeen hundred vertical feet in its first mile, with few switchbacks - to a ridge saddle near Point 5116. From the saddle the route climbs roughly a thousand feet to Peak 5791, then traverses heather benches and meadows above the lake, crossing or contouring Peak 5860, to reach the base of the east ridge.

ways.name: Camping at the lake below the ridge
ways.season: Same window
ways.notes: The lake below the ridge is the common overnight for this route and turns it from a very long day into a comfortable two. The camping is in the meadows on the lake's east side and there is reliable water. Parties doing it in a day still pass through the same ground and should treat the lake as the last water before the ridge.

ways.name: Mowich Lake, Spray Park and the Ptarmigan crest
ways.season: June to early July
ways.notes: The prettier of the two ways in, and the one that puts you on the route's own ridge from the bottom. Mowich Lake sits at about 4,929 ft at the end of a road that has had no public access since the SR 165 Fairfax Bridge closed in April 2025 (before that it was often snowed shut into early or mid July), and that single fact decides whether this approach is available at all. From the lake it is three to four miles of trail up through Spray Park; at about 6,400 ft a beaten path breaks off right toward the permanent snow. Cross the Flett Glacier in the gap between Echo Rock, 7,870 ft, and Observation Rock, 8,364 ft, at somewhere around 7,500 ft, climb to the saddle immediately east of Observation Rock, and cross onto the Russell Glacier near 7,800 ft. From there the crest runs south, sometimes on rock but mostly on easy snow just left of the crest line, with the Russell falling away east. This stretch is uncrevassed and is genuinely a walk. The last few hundred yards to camp are not: the crest narrows to a knife edge with an overhanging rock step on it, and most parties bypass that by dropping about 200 ft onto 40 degree snow on the east side and traversing back. Well above the base, the exit gully through the rock buttress is the one identification climbers argue about — whether it is the first or the second break in the cliffs is genuinely unsettled, so climb to the fixed pin rather than to a count. The descent is the Emmons route out to White River, so coming in this way needs a car shuttle or a very long road walk.

ways.name: White River, St. Elmo Pass and across the Carbon
ways.season: Mid-May to early July
ways.notes: The way in that is actually available during the ice season, because the White River road opens in late spring while Mowich Lake has had no road access since the 2025 bridge closure, and it puts you back at your own car after the Emmons descent instead of on the far side of the mountain. It is the Liberty Ridge approach as far as the Carbon: Glacier Basin, then a boot track up snow and scree to St. Elmo Pass, given variously as 7,400 or 7,600 ft, then onto the Winthrop Glacier and a roped traverse at roughly 7,200 to 7,400 ft around to Curtis Ridge, where there are good bivy sites near 7,500 ft. Next morning drop and cross the Carbon around 7,000 ft, staying clear of its seracs and north of the ice cliffs where the Russell calves onto it, then take snowfields up onto the Ptarmigan crest at about its 9,000 ft point and follow the ridge to high camp. It is longer than the Mowich walk, it crosses three glaciers, and it spends hours under actively shedding walls, so it wants to be done cold and early. One thing to fix in your head before the descent: parties coming off Liberty Cap routes routinely wander onto the busy Disappointment Cleaver at Columbia Crest instead of the faint Emmons track, which is the wrong side of the mountain if your car is at White River.

ways.name: Lake Constance climbers' trail, then up Avalanche Canyon past the South Chute
ways.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Snow in the chute is an improvement on the scree, but Avalanche Canyon is named for what runs down it in May and June
ways.notes:
Bike or walk the closed Dosewallips Road (FS 2610) about 5 miles to the Lake Constance climbers' trail, then the steep, unmaintained trail roughly 3,300 ft in under 2.2 miles to Lake Constance at 4,800 ft. Camp at the north end of the lake.

From the lake, head north into Avalanche Canyon. This route is the parallel couloir further into the canyon: where the standard South Chute line turns east and climbs out early, the North Chute keeps you in the canyon bed longer and climbs from higher up it.

It sees less traffic than the South Chute and is commonly used as one half of a loop — up one, down the other — rather than as a route in its own right. It rejoins the standard line where the South Chute's gully tops out, crosses the Finger Traverse (or the Terrible Traverse when conditions allow), and finishes over the summit block and the North Chimney.

ways.name: Dosewallips road and Constance Pass, over Crystal Pass into upper Avalanche Canyon
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
ways.notes: The alternative that avoids the Lake Constance trail. Road-walk or bike roughly 6.5 miles from the washout past the Lake Constance turn-off to the road end at the old campground and ranger station, then the Constance Pass Trail south and southwest to Constance Pass at about 5,850 ft. Leave the trail, travel cross-country west into the head of Crystal Basin, and climb to Crystal Pass on the Constance-Warrior massif. From Crystal Pass drop south into upper Avalanche Canyon. This is the variant that suits this route best of the three Constance routes, because the North Chute is the higher of the two chutes and coming in from Crystal Pass you meet it without walking the whole canyon up from the lake.

ways.name: White Salmon Lodge road (standard)
ways.season: spring to early summer; needs snow cover
ways.notes:
Pull off at the old White Salmon lodge site on the Mount Baker Highway, walk around the gate, and follow the old road past the lodge for about a mile to where it finishes in an old clearcut.

What you do next depends entirely on snow cover, and getting this wrong is the single biggest time sink on the approach. With good cover, drop northeast off the clearcut down to White Salmon Creek and walk the valley toward the toe of the White Salmon Glacier — pleasant going. Without good cover, do not descend into the valley at all: hold your elevation as you enter the clearcut and contour around instead, giving up height only where a rock band or a stream crossing forces it. The valley bottom without snow is slide alder and devil's club.

From the glacier area, the route continues up toward the shoulder at the foot of the face.

ways.name: Mount Baker Ski Area (Chair 8) traverse
ways.season: winter/spring, on skis
ways.notes: An alternative used mainly by ski parties: start at the base of Chair 8 in the ski area and make a downhill traverse into the bottom of the White Salmon Creek valley, then climb over four thousand feet up the glacier. It removes the clearcut and the road walk at the cost of a long climb from the valley floor and a committing descent to start the day.

ways.name: Downey Creek and Bachelor Creek to the ridge camp, then across onto the northern icefield
ways.season: Late July through September for the approach; the face itself favours a firm, cold night
ways.notes:
The walk-in is the standard route's: Trail #768 six and a half miles to the camp at about 2,440 ft, then the unmaintained Bachelor Creek path, a ford to the south side near 3,700 ft, the old avalanche-debris zone near 4,500 ft where the tread disappears into slide alder and downed timber, a pass near 5,900 ft, a lake at about 5,338 ft, and a high camp on the ridge above between roughly 6,400 and 6,900 ft.

From camp the difference begins: continue over the col between the two glaciers at about 8,500 ft and descend onto the larger northern icefield, then traverse beneath the peak's north side to reach the foot of the face.

ways.name: From the col to the west, traversing the icefield from that side
ways.season: Midsummer through early autumn, and only as part of a larger traverse of the range
ways.notes: The first ascent came at the face from the other direction, from the col to the west, traversing the northern icefield across to the peak. That is the natural line for a party already high in this range on a multi-peak traverse rather than for a party walking in for this route alone; it involves no new trailhead but a great deal more glacier travel, and it should be planned as one leg of a bigger trip.

ways.name: North Fork Sauk Trail and the PCT over Red Pass
ways.season: Jun-Aug
ways.notes: The way in since the White Chuck side closed. North Fork Sauk Trail #649 runs up the valley through old growth to Mackinaw Shelter and then switchbacks steeply to the Pacific Crest Trail at about 5,950 ft, roughly eight to nine miles from the trailhead. Turn north on the PCT, cross Red Pass a mile or two on, and descend into the upper White Chuck valley, following the PCT down it for roughly seven to nine miles past the old White Chuck River Trail junction to Sitkum Creek. It is much longer than the old approach, and the climb back over Red Pass comes on the way out.

ways.name: White Chuck River Trail #643 (closed since the 2003 flood)
ways.season: Jun-Aug
ways.notes:
This was the standard way up Glacier Peak until the October 2003 flood. The White Chuck Road (FR 23) is now closed to vehicles at milepost 3.7 and the trail has been listed as inaccessible since the flood, so this is kept as a record of the old line rather than as a way in.

From the trailhead at about 2,350 ft the trail runs upstream through old growth, crossing Pumice, Glacier and Kennedy Creeks — reliable water, but high with snowmelt in early summer. At about five and a half miles is the old Kennedy Hot Springs area at around 3,300 ft, still a popular campsite; the pool, lodge and guard station were destroyed by the 2003 flood and never rebuilt, so there is no usable hot pool there.

Another mile and a half brings you to Sitkum Creek and the PCT junction at about 3,850 ft. Turn north on the PCT for about half a mile to a forested camp near 4,100 ft.

ways.name: Buck Creek Trail to Pass No Pass
ways.season: Midsummer into early autumn, once the high meadows melt out. The alternative grass-and-heather line is likely hazardous when wet.
ways.notes: From the highway junction take the state route north, then the loop road and the Chiwawa River Road (Forest Road 6200) to its end at the Trinity trailhead. Check current road status before committing to the drive: the road has been closed to vehicles well below the trailhead, which cuts off drive-in access entirely. From the trailhead hike the Buck Creek trail, climbing steadily through forest and along the creek to about 5,600 ft, where the standard line breaks off to the right. This is normally done as part of a backpacking trip to the pass rather than in a day, and the peak sits about half a mile northeast of that pass on the crest.

ways.name: Buck Creek Pass and the grass slopes
ways.season: Midsummer into early autumn on dry ground only — this line is likely hazardous when the grass and heather are wet.
ways.notes: The alternative stays on the trail past the off-trail turn and continues all the way to Buck Creek Pass itself, then climbs steep grass and heather slopes from the pass to the west side of the summit block before the same short scramble to the top. It is the option for a party already camped at the pass on a backpacking trip, and it trades the braided boot path and the meadow traverse for a steeper direct climb.

ways.name: East Bank Trail on foot from milepost 138, leaving it at May Creek
ways.season: Late May through July while the headwall is still a snow climb; the highway gate closes the season at both ends
ways.notes: Park at the East Bank Trailhead near milepost 138 at about 1,800 ft. The trail drops immediately to the bridge over Ruby Creek and then runs north along Ross Lake, mostly flat and fast, to the May Creek camp. This is the whole of the easy walking. At May Creek leave the trail and climb east, staying loosely between the creeks on the mountain's west side. Cliff bands start around 3,200 ft and are threaded on boot and game trails rather than climbed; snow generally begins around 4,800 to 5,000 ft. Three miles or so of that work reaches a flat camp just over 5,200 ft below the toe of the ice. Strong parties carry a second camp onto the upper glacier near 7,400 ft, which shortens summit day considerably.

ways.name: Water taxi up Ross Lake to the eastern shore, cutting out most of the trail
ways.season: Same window as the trail approach, but only once the boat service is running for the year
ways.notes: The resort at the south end of Ross Lake runs a water taxi that will drop parties on the eastern shore, which removes most of the flat trail miles and turns the approach into the off-trail climb alone. It has to be booked ahead and the schedule and drop points change, so confirm directly before building a trip around it. The trade is that you are committed to a pickup time on a lake with no road out, so build slack into the plan rather than into the summit day.

ways.name: Before the highway opens: the gate at milepost 134
ways.season: Late winter and early spring, before the highway is cleared, when the headwall holds its best snow
ways.notes: The highway closes each winter between the gate west of the trailhead and a second gate far to the east, and reopens somewhere between mid-April and early summer depending on the year's damage and snowpack. Parties wanting the headwall in condition have started at the closed gate and covered the road on bikes or skis to the trailhead before starting the walk in. Everything above that is unchanged, except that the snow line is far lower and the timber belt may go faster on skis than it does on foot in summer.

ways.name: Colchuck Lake outlet into the west cirque
ways.season: Jul-Sep
ways.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead (NF-7601 off Icicle Creek Road; Northwest Forest Pass). Trail #1599 for about 2.25 miles, crossing Mountaineer Creek on a log bridge near the 1.5-mile mark, to the signed junction where Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A splits left. Cross Mountaineer Creek a second time on a log bridge, then climb steepening rocky switchbacks to Colchuck Lake — about 4 miles and 2,280 ft, roughly one and three-quarter to three hours depending on load.

Colchuck Lake is the last reliable water; the basin and the wall are dry, though a spring at the base of the boulder field below the formation has been reported and should not be relied on.

The shorter of the two ways into the west basin: from the lake's north end, cross the outlet below the small dam and follow a climbers' path up and across the timbered hillside directly into the cirque below the wall — about an hour from the lake, plus 15 to 25 minutes of boulder-hopping to reach the actual base.

ways.name: Aasgard-side lakeshore, slide alder, leftmost gully
ways.season: Jul-Sep; ice axe useful before mid-July
ways.notes:
The longer southern option, which avoids the outlet crossing. From Colchuck Lake follow the lakeshore climbers' path counter-clockwise toward the slopes below Aasgard Pass, gaining talus and heather to roughly 400 ft above the lake in 30 to 40 minutes. That slope holds wet snow into July and has a real slip-and-fall history.

Cut north / climber's-left off the Aasgard trail through a band of dense slide alder and heather — genuinely a bushwhack, 15 to 20 minutes, with a cairned path through it if you can find it. Once past the alder, take the left-most gully and climb it about 1,000 ft to its top, then contour east on an easy path into the west basin. One and a half to two hours from the lake.

ways.name: Middle Fork Snoqualmie to Dutch Miller Gap
ways.season: July to September; recorded ascents cluster in August and September. The upper cirque holds snow well into summer, so carry an axe.
ways.notes: The standard way. From the Middle Fork Snoqualmie road end, follow the Dutch Miller Gap trail up the valley for a long day — roughly fourteen to fifteen miles — passing the horse camp and the Williams Lake trail junction on the way to the gap. Most parties break this over two days and camp near Williams Lake or at the gap. There is no cross-country detour for this route: stay on the trail to the top.

ways.name: Necklace Valley and La Bohn Gap from the north
ways.season: July to September.
ways.notes: A longer alternative from the other side of the divide: the Necklace Valley trail off the Foss River road, over La Bohn Gap, then down to Dutch Miller Gap. It joins the standard line at the gap, so everything above is identical. Worth knowing about mainly as a through-trip option or if the Middle Fork road end is not usable.

ways.name: Pete Lake and Summit Chief camp from the east
ways.season: July to September.
ways.notes: The eastern option, from a camp near Pete Lake and Summit Chief. It does not reach Dutch Miller Gap at all — it comes at the peak's northeast basin from the other side and joins the route higher up. It is the approach that puts the ridge notch in your path, which the trail-to-the-gap line avoids.

ways.name: Waptus River and Lake Ivanhoe from Salmon La Sac
ways.season: July to September. The river ford and the lakeshore snow are both much more serious during snowmelt.
ways.notes: The long southeastern way in, usually spread over two or three days. From the Salmon La Sac road end north of Cle Elum, follow the Waptus River trail up its gentle valley to Waptus Lake, roughly nine miles. The old hiker bridge over the river below the lake is gone, so this is a real ford, about knee deep at normal summer flow. Past the lake the trail follows the southeast shore, which can hold steep snow into early summer, to a ford of Chief Creek near the head of the lake, about twelve miles from the car. From Chief Creek the Dutch Miller Gap trail switchbacks up the forested slope, passes Lake Ivanhoe and reaches the gap, roughly five more miles and about 2,000 ft higher. At the gap it meets the standard approach, and the climbing above is the same.

ways.name: Upper Dungeness Trail to Home Lake and Constance Pass
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Oct per NPS guidance for the Constance Pass and Home Lake corridor; earlier trips should expect lingering snow
ways.notes:
From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead at about 2,880 ft at the end of FR 2870, follow Upper Dungeness Trail #833.2 south along the Dungeness River. The first mile is mostly flat; stay left at the Royal Basin Trail junction near a mile. Camp Handy — riverside meadow with a cedar shingle shelter — comes at about 3.4 miles.

Just past Camp Handy the trail forks; take the uphill fork and begin a sustained, largely switchback-free climb of about 3 miles and 1,800 ft to Boulder Shelter at 6.4 miles and about 4,890 ft. The creek there is the most reliable water on the whole approach — treat it as the last sure fill-up. Bear right at the shelter onto the Home Lake / Constance Pass Trail. The park boundary is about a mile beyond, after which brush closes in from both sides.

The final 2.9 miles to Home Lake at 5,330 ft, roughly 9.3-9.6 miles from the trailhead, climb another 700-900 ft through subalpine forest into heather meadows, crossing two or three small streams; one waterfall crossing is awkward to keep feet dry and is slick with a full pack early season. Home Lake is the standard basecamp for Fricaba, Hal Foss, Mystery and Deception.

From camp continue on climbers' paths — no maintained tread — up to Constance Pass at about 5,750-5,800 ft, then traverse and descend west into upper Deception Basin.

ways.name: Royal Basin and the Royal-Deception divide into Deception Basin
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
ways.notes:
The other way into the same basin, and the one that suits a party doing Fricaba alongside Mystery and Deception. From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead take Trail #833.2 about a mile and bear right onto the Royal Basin Trail #832 at the fork just before the Royal Creek footlog bridge. Royal Lake at about 7.2 miles and 5,100 ft is the basecamp; upper Royal Basin camps sit around 5,800-6,200 ft.

From upper Royal Basin climb the moraine and a 35-40 degree snowfield to the notch on the Royal-Deception divide at about 6,500-6,560 ft, then descend scree to the grass and heather benches above Deception Basin. Fricaba is then across the basin to the east.

One published day-2 description of this side has parties angling up toward the pass going east for Fricaba, then round to the left of some gendarmes and up a steep scree route the account calls self-explanatory.

ways.name: Mount Pilchuck Road to the trailhead
ways.season: July to October. The trail is typically snow-covered into early or midsummer in some years, and traction is commonly needed through June.
ways.notes: From Granite Falls take the highway east and then the Mountain Loop about ten or eleven miles to the ranger station. Continue about a mile past it, cross the river, and turn south onto the Mount Pilchuck road. Follow it roughly seven miles — a mix of paved and rough washboarded gravel that varies year to year with maintenance — to the trailhead parking area at around three thousand feet.

ways.name: From the Heather Lake trailhead when the road is gated
ways.season: Shoulder season, when the forest road is closed below the trailhead — common in spring and autumn.
ways.notes: In years when the road is gated below the trailhead, the walk starts from the Heather Lake trailhead instead, adding roughly five miles and substantial gain each way. Everything above the normal trailhead is identical, so this is a road-walk variant rather than a different climb, but it changes a half-day into a long one and is worth confirming before driving out.

ways.name: White Salmon Creek from the old lodge site, up the White Salmon Glacier to the dividing shoulder
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Aug. Earlier the valley is snow-covered and simpler but the true North Face above you sheds avalanches; later the crevasses on the White Salmon are open and the lower valley is alder
ways.notes: Get the backcountry permit at the Glacier Public Service Center on the way in — it is required, not advisory. Then continue up the Mount Baker Highway to the pull-off at the old White Salmon Lodge site, walk round the gate, and follow the old roadbed roughly a mile to where it ends at an old clearcut. From the road-end, with adequate snow cover, drop northeast off-trail to White Salmon Creek and follow the valley up toward the toe of the White Salmon Glacier. Roped travel usually begins at the toe, and the crevasse hazard grows through the season. Ascend glacier and moraine to a bivy below the first rock and ice barrier. Published bivy elevations for this route disagree by around a thousand feet — so the honest instruction is to camp at the rock outcrops on the eastern edge of the White Salmon, where the ridge meets the face, rather than at a number. The Hanging Glacier and North Face approach is in the White Salmon Creek drainage, one valley west of Price Lake — not on the Nooksack and Ruth Creek side of the mountain.

ways.name: Fisher Chimneys and Winnie's Slide, then down the White Salmon Glacier to the base
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Aug, once the Lake Ann trail is out from under snow
ways.notes:
The alternative used by parties who would rather start from the standard trailhead than from the White Salmon roadbed: from the Lake Ann Trailhead on SR-542, climb the Fisher Chimneys and Winnie's Slide to a bivy near the Upper Curtis Glacier, then descend about 1,000 ft down the White Salmon Glacier and traverse the northwest rib to reach the foot of the Hanging Glacier.

It is longer in vertical terms because it climbs to a camp and then gives back a thousand feet, and it commits you to regaining that thousand feet on the way out if you return the same way. Its advantage is a maintained trail to a known camp instead of a valley bushwhack, and it does not require the White Salmon roadbed to be walkable.

No trailhead-to-base time is given for this variant; published figures for it vary too much to quote one.

ways.name: From Ross Lake by boat and up Silver Creek to the lake basin camp
ways.season: Late July through September
ways.notes: Book a water taxi for the long run up Ross Lake and get dropped at the mouth of Silver Creek at about 1,600 ft. A trail climbs the north side of the creek roughly two and a half miles to an old cabin at about 2,900 ft; above that the route is cross-country with occasional blazes, across slide alder and forest slopes, to the camp in the Silver Lake basin at about 6,763 ft. This is the shorter side for this particular route and it keeps the whole trip inside the United States, at the cost of depending on a boat.

ways.name: Depot Creek from the north side of the border, over the col between the two peaks
ways.season: Late July through September, and only with passports
ways.notes: The other way in starts on the Canadian side: a rough spur off the lake road to a washout at about 2,600 ft, an overgrown roadbed to the boundary obelisk and register, and then the climbers' path up the creek through old growth to the falls, whose wet slabs and old fixed hand-line are the crux of the walk-in. Above them the path leads to the lake camp at about 5,700 ft. From that camp the way to this route climbs toward and over the col between the two peaks rather than onto the south-west side.

ways.name: Andrews Creek trail #504 from the Chewuch River road
ways.season: Roughly mid-July through September, once the trails and the face have shed snow
ways.notes:
Drive north from Winthrop up the Chewuch River road to the Andrews Creek trailhead at about 3,050 ft. This is the shortest drive of the three ways in and it is paved the whole way.

Walk Andrews Creek trail #504 up the drainage. The lower miles cross an old burn, so there is almost no shade, the tread is overgrown and soaks you after rain, and blowdown is normal. Andrews Creek runs beside the trail for that whole stretch and is reliable water. The trail tops out at Andrews Pass above 6,680 ft, where the burn gives way to open parkland.

From the pass continue on the Boundary Trail #533 and drop on the Cathedral Lakes side trail to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft. Bear off near the old wilderness guard-station cabin. Strong parties walk it in one long day with heavy packs; others split it with a camp partway up the drainage.

One thing to leave alone: there is a shorter-looking way in from the Canadian side. Crossing into the United States here is illegal, the border is patrolled, and the penalties are severe.

ways.name: Cathedral Driveway trail #510A from Loomis via Toats Coulee
ways.season: Roughly mid-July through September
ways.notes:
This is a trail, #510A, not a four-wheel-drive road, despite a persistent claim to the contrary — the high-clearance warning in circulation belongs to a different spur road. Access is from Loomis by Toats Coulee Road, then a Y junction, then the forest roads up to the trailhead at about 5,570 ft.

Be careful with the trailhead name. It appears in print under three or four spellings, and one of those names also belongs to a completely different trailhead near Winthrop. Navigate to the road, not to the name.

The trail descends from its high trailhead to join the valley trail below, and from there it is the valley to the Cathedral Lakes basin. This is the shortest walk and the least climbing of the ways in.

The catch sits at both ends. The drive is about two hours longer than from Winthrop, and because the trailhead is high and the trail drops to meet the valley, you finish the trip with roughly 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out, at the point when you least want it.

ways.name: Thirtymile Trailhead and the Chewuch River trail toward Remmel Lake
ways.notes: Follow the Chewuch River trail north from the Thirtymile Trailhead nearly to Remmel Lake, then climb to the Cathedral Lakes basin. A longer way round than Andrews Creek, used when combining the Remmel Lake country with the climb.

ways.name: FR-2419 up the Big Creek drainage to the road-end trailhead
ways.season: Roughly Jun-Sep, best Jul-Sep. Spring and early summer put avalanche-capable snow in the gully
ways.notes:
From the T-intersection at the end of North Lake Cushman Road, go right onto FS Road 24 for about 1.5 miles, then left onto FS Road 2419 and follow it up the Big Creek drainage roughly 6.6 miles to its end at a small trailhead at about 3,026 ft. Northwest Forest Pass to park; no wilderness permit is needed.

From here the trail quickly becomes a boot path and then largely off-trail scrambling — there is no numbered maintained trail for most of the route. It climbs directly and steeply through forest, hand-over-hand on roots and rock in places, to a couple of open meadow benches around 3,800 ft. That meadow band holds the most reliable early-season water via snowmelt seeps; by mid-to-late summer expect it dry, so carry what you need from the car.

ways.name: From Mount Ellinor, across the connecting ridge or the west-side basin
ways.season: Roughly Jun-Sep
ways.notes: Recorded as an approach because parties do reach Washington from Ellinor rather than from Big Creek, usually as half of a traverse. Ellinor is reached by Trail #812 from its Upper or Lower Trailhead, both on the same North Lake Cushman Road corridor, and from Ellinor's summit the connecting ridge runs northeast toward Washington. It is not a walk. The crest is fractured, weathered pillow basalt with sustained Class 4 scrambling past a series of gendarmes, and it carries a loose 50 ft downclimb that most parties call the least enjoyable part of the day. The alternative that several parties prefer is the west-side basin traverse: drop into the basin below the crest and cross it, rejoining Ellinor's standard winter route line rather than fighting the ridge. Used as an approach to Washington this is a long way round for a peak with a 3.2 km trail of its own, and it is here for traverse parties.

ways.name: Cascade Pass Trail and Sahale Arm to Sahale Glacier Camp
ways.season: Jul-Sep
ways.notes: Cascade River Road runs about 22-23 miles from Marblemount to the Cascade Pass trailhead, a large lot at road's end at 3,600 ft. This is the only approach on this list that is on maintained trail almost the whole way. The Cascade Pass Trail switchbacks up through old-growth timber — roughly 35 switchbacks, about 1,800 ft in the first two miles — then eases through meadows to Cascade Pass at about 5,400 ft, 3.5-3.7 miles in. At the pass take the left (north) fork for Sahale Arm and switchback up the open ridge crest, about another 2.1-2.2 miles and 2,200 ft, to Sahale Glacier Camp at roughly 7,200-7,600 ft — rock-walled tent pads on the moraine, and the NPS-permitted high camp. Water is reliable at the creek crossings low on the trail, at Doubtful Lake (a signed spur, about a mile and 1,000 ft down and back) and from snowmelt near Sahale Glacier Camp early and mid season. Sources dry up late summer, so fill before the long switchback climb. Above camp the Sahale Glacier is small and low-angle by North Cascades standards but should still be treated as a glacier — rope up rather than assuming it out. Overnight camping is quota-limited and needs a North Cascades backcountry permit picked up in person at Marblemount.

ways.name: Car-to-car day push
ways.season: Jul-Sep, long daylight
ways.notes:
Because the approach is on maintained trail to about 7,200 ft, Sahale is regularly done in a single long day from the trailhead, which sidesteps the quota-limited high camp entirely. The trade is that you carry glacier gear the whole 6 miles up and 6 miles down, and you meet the summit block later in the day when it is busiest and the snow is softest.

Nothing about the line changes; only the logistics do. If the permit lottery has closed you out of Sahale Glacier Camp, this is the fallback rather than a different route.

ways.name: Tunnel Creek trail to the crest trail at the lake, then south to the pass
ways.season: July through September, once the crest trail is clear
ways.notes:
From the forest road east of Skykomish, the Tunnel Creek trail climbs about eleven hundred and seventy feet in under a mile and a half from roughly 3,100 ft to a small lake on the crest, where it meets the long-distance crest trail. Turn south and follow that trail several miles to the pass at roughly 5,800 ft.

This is the option with the least climbing and the easiest tread. It is a little longer along the crest than the other trailhead, and the walking is straightforward the whole way, which makes it the better choice with heavy loads or a late start.

ways.name: Surprise Creek trail past the two lakes, then the switchbacks to the pass
ways.season: July through September
ways.notes:
The other trailhead climbs the Surprise Creek trail past the first lake at about 4,500 ft and its neighbour, then switchbacks up to the same pass. It is roughly a mile shorter to the pass than the crest-trail option and costs several hundred feet more climbing, and it is in the trees for essentially the whole way, so it gives less to look at and less warning of the weather ahead.

Both trailheads meet at the pass and nothing above it differs.

ways.name: Spire Gully from the SR-20 hairpin (dry)
ways.season: Jul-Sep
ways.notes:
Park at the dirt pullout on the obvious hairpin turn on SR-20, directly beneath the east faces of the two Early Winters Spires. Do not use the Blue Lake Trailhead — that is the west-side approach and it puts you on the wrong side of the mountain.

Walk up the obvious gully, which is the easy way through the first band of cliffs above the road. Above that cliff band a faint climbers' path leaves the gully on a gently rising line to the right, crossing easy slabs and vegetated dirt. Roughly three quarters of an hour out you come to some fourth-class slabs.

The classic sequence of landmarks, and the one to hold in your head: up Spire Gully following occasional cairns to the last big tree in the middle of the gully; from that tree traverse right across talus; that brings you under the gully that runs up to the notch between North and South Early Winters Spires; then traverse left to the foot of the buttress.

The whole line is visible from the road, so look up and read it before you start walking.

ways.name: Early-season, snow in Spire Gully
ways.season: Highway opening through Jun
ways.notes: Same line from the hairpin, but with snow in Spire Gully the traverse right from the last big tree is done on snow rather than talus. Crampons and an axe are worth carrying; sources on this approach say so explicitly for the early season. SR-20 is gated over Washington Pass through the winter, typically from late November or early December to mid-April or early May, so this window opens with the highway.

ways.name: Pete Lake and the PCT switchbacks to the Vista Lakes tarns
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, but see the moat note — the gate at 7,000 ft can shut by mid-July, earlier in a thin snow year
ways.notes:
Walk the Pete Lake trail #1323 up the Cooper River to a fork at about 3,120 ft, roughly five miles in. Turn right, continue about six tenths of a mile, and turn right again onto the Pacific Crest Trail at about 3,220 ft. Follow the PCT four and a half miles up a long series of switchbacks to about 5,500 ft.

The Vista Lakes tarns lie east of the trail at that height and hold the good bivy sites. Summit Chief is about two more miles from there. Reported times from the car to the upper lake run to most of a day with overnight loads, and every published account treats this as a two- or three-day trip.

This is also the last reliable water. The ground above is reported bone dry until you come back down to the lakes.

From camp, leave the PCT and traverse cross-country toward Summit Chief Pass, then follow the ridge north-west staying below the cliffs and gendarmes, into the upper basin south-east of the main summit. One party's hindsight on this traverse is worth having: they should have dropped to about 6,000 ft and taken the scree instead of holding height across steep sloping slabs.

ways.name: Lemah Meadow shortcut, cutting the PCT switchbacks
ways.season: Same window; the bypass is brushier and is a trade of distance for thrashing
ways.notes: A recorded variant that saves about three miles. After gaining roughly a thousand feet on the tight PCT switchbacks, leave the trail at the corner around 4,000 ft and head north, climbing about six hundred feet to the crest. The party who did it found plenty of windfall and pockets of vine maple, and called it irritating rather than difficult. It is a single-source variant, so treat the line as a hint rather than a route.

ways.name: Snow Lake Trail to Great Scott Bowl and Pineapple Pass
ways.season: Jul-Sep (snow-free)
ways.notes: Upper Alpental lot at the end of Alpental Road (about 3,100 ft), I-90 exit 52. Take the Snow Lake Trail (#1013) north; a cat track runs up the valley from the end of the lot, just left of the stream, before the tread narrows to normal trail. At roughly 1.5-1.6 miles a small signed junction splits Source Lake from Snow Lake — bear left toward Source Lake. Cross the Source Lake basin contouring near 4,000 ft, then at about 4,400 ft you crest a lip and drop into Great Scott Bowl (also called Pineapple Basin). Work up the bowl on talus, or on snow if any remains, toward Pineapple Pass at the head of it, passing beneath the Fang — the pinnacle on the bowl's west side that carries the Edge of Time route. The common error is here, not lower down: a boot path running around the back of the Fang leads into the gully between the Fang and the Tooth. Parties who take it have to backtrack several hundred feet through trees and rock fields to get back onto the right ground. The second error is going straight up to Pineapple Pass itself — that col is the rappel line down, not the way up.

ways.name: Winter and spring, snow-covered Alpental valley
ways.season: winter to early summer, snow
ways.notes: Once there is meaningful snow the summer tread is not the route. The talus slopes the summer trail crosses are the Alpental valley's avalanche chutes — seventeen of them are counted along its length — and the winter line instead climbs the valley on the south side of the South Fork Snoqualmie toward Source Lake rather than following the summer switchbacks across those paths. From below Source Lake, traverse up into Great Scott Bowl, typically on an upward-traversing line on the west side of the bowl passing beneath the Fang, and join whatever track leads to Pineapple Pass. Most parties cache skis or snowshoes in the bowl before the final slope. The entire trip through the Source Lake and Snow Lake basins is avalanche terrain; this is a stability decision, not a route-finding one.

ways.name: Upper Dungeness Trail, Camp Handy and Boulder Shelter to the southeast cirque
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. Snow in the summit couloir into early season is an improvement on the scree that replaces it
ways.notes:
From US-101 near Sequim Bay State Park turn on Louella Road for a mile, then Palo Alto Road for about 5.8 miles, becoming FS Road 28 at the forest boundary. Right on FS 2880 past Dungeness Forks Campground, then left on FS 2870 for 8.7 miles to the Upper Dungeness Trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass required at the kiosk.

Trail #833.2 is the shortest and easiest approach. Hike 3.2-3.4 miles and about 600 ft to Camp Handy at roughly 3,100 ft, a riverfront meadow with a cedar-shingle shelter, then take the uphill fork and continue about 3 miles and 1,850 ft to Boulder Camp / Boulder Shelter at 6.3-6.4 miles and roughly 4,890-4,950 ft. The creek there is the most reliable water on the approach.

From Boulder Shelter hike south on the Dungeness / Constance Pass trail, crossing several creeks, toward Home Lake.

ways.name: Home Lake basecamp, from either the Dungeness or the Dosewallips side
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
ways.notes:
Home Lake at about 5,308-5,330 ft, walled in by Mount Constance and Warrior Peak just below Constance Pass, is the standard basecamp for this climb and it is reachable from two directions: north up the Upper Dungeness / Constance Pass trail at roughly 9.3 miles from the Upper Dungeness Trailhead, or south from the Dosewallips road end over Constance Pass. An Olympic National Park wilderness permit is required.

Camping at Home Lake rather than pushing from Boulder Shelter turns this into a comfortable two-day trip and puts you a mile from the cirque. It is also the camp shared with Mount Fricaba, Mount Mystery and Mount Deception parties, so it is well-used ground with an established site.

From the lake, leave the basin and climb east into the Warrior / Inner Constance cirque through meadow and talus.

ways.name: Hannegan Pass and the Chilliwack River Trail to Bear Creek
ways.season: Late July through September, once the Chilliwack crossing has dropped and the buttress is dry
ways.notes:
From the road end at about 3,100 ft, Trail #674 runs nearly level for the first mile and then climbs at a steady grade to Hannegan Pass at about 5,100 ft. Drop off the east side and continue down into the Chilliwack valley, bearing right at the park boundary onto the Chilliwack River Trail proper. The tread loses height past a backcountry camp to the Chilliwack River crossing - historically a hand-pulled cable car, and a serious ford if it is not running, so check its status before you plan around it - then runs down-valley past further camps to the Bear Creek confluence. The camp at that confluence has been closed since fire came through the drainage, so confirm it is open rather than assuming a bed there.

At Bear Creek the maintained trail ends. Ford the creek, which can be a genuinely committing crossing in snowmelt, and climb steep brushy timber eastward; higher the brush turns to huckleberry and slide alder before opening into meadows above Ruta Lake. Traverse the divide from there, skirting the loose south-facing slopes below two unnamed points and crossing a rock rib, to a broad saddle at about 6,480 ft with running water and heather tent sites. Most parties split this over two days.

ways.name: From the Chilliwack Lake road on the Canadian side
ways.season: Same window, and only if the border crossing is confirmed lawful
ways.notes: There is a far shorter line to the same camp from the road on the Canadian side of the border - a fraction of the distance the Hannegan approach covers. It crosses the border on foot where there is no port of entry, and this page cannot say that crossing is lawful, so confirm it with the border authorities before planning on it; and the tread turns unmaintained and badly overgrown after the first mile or two, so the miles it saves are not all easy ones. Most parties starting in the United States take the long way rather than deal with it; parties already north of the border have the opposite calculation.

ways.name: Ross Lake boat crossing, Lightning Creek trail and the abandoned Freezeout Creek trail
ways.season: Late July through September in a normal year; the creek is hard to ford until the snowmelt drops
ways.notes:
This is the way in that stays entirely inside the United States, and it is the reason the peak costs three or four days.

From the highway pullout above the dam, a short spur trail drops to the lake shore. Cross the lake by water taxi, or paddle a private or inflatable boat portaged down that spur, and land near the head of the lake where the Lightning Creek trail starts at about 1,500 ft. Parties with their own boat commonly start walking around four in the morning to leave daylight for the day above; the water taxi runs only in the daytime, 8am to 5pm.

After a couple of hours watch for the junction with the old, no-longer-maintained Freezeout Creek trail. The stretch immediately above that junction is the hardest navigation of the entire approach: steep rock and alder slopes that want a rising, diagonal line before you regain forest and real tread. Intermittent orange flagging marks it and is worth hunting for.

Back in the trees the tread improves up to a cabin at about 3,600 ft, sited just after a creek crossing — bunks, a wood stove and a logbook, and a useful emergency shelter. About a quarter mile past it, cross the creek again and pass through an old burn. Tread mostly disappears around 4,200 ft.

The lower part of this corridor is national recreation area and needs a park backcountry permit for camping; above the boundary it is wilderness with a free self-issue permit.

ways.name: The crest trail north from Harts Pass to Castle Pass
ways.season: Late July through September, once the high road is open and the traverse is clear of snow
ways.notes:
The third way in, and the one that trades a boat for a great deal of walking. The high pass road climbs roughly twenty miles of unpaved single lane from Mazama with pullouts rather than passing room, a rock wall on one side and an unguarded drop on the other, and grades approaching seventeen percent on the upper ramps. Trailers are prohibited and wide vehicles are strongly discouraged. It opens with the snowmelt, typically early to mid July, and closes with the first serious autumn storms.

From the pass, the crest trail runs north through country that starts near 6,200 ft and barely drops below 5,000 ft, over a high pass and on to Castle Pass, where it meets the Boundary Trail running east across the Pasayten and west toward the lake. Camps along the way are open and windy; pitch behind timber rather than in the meadow.

This stays inside the United States throughout, and it needs no boat.

ways.name: Trinity and the Chiwawa River Trail to Chiwawa Basin and the 6,300 ft benches
ways.season: Late Jun-Sep. The road to Trinity is often not melted out until mid-June, and the upper mountain and col hold snow into July in heavy years
ways.notes:
Park at Trinity Trailhead near 2,800 ft at the end of Chiwawa River Road/FR-6200 by the old mine site. Start up-valley on Buck Creek Trail #1513 for about a mile and a half and bear right at the fork onto Chiwawa River Trail #1550, which takes over an old mining-road grade close to the river — water is reliable along all of this.

About 3.7 more miles brings the signed Red Mountain Trail junction near 4,000 ft. This is the last water that is both obvious and easy to reach before the basin, so fill here. Bear left into Chiwawa Basin rather than taking the right-hand switchbacks up Red Mountain.

Beyond the junction the tread deteriorates, braids and climbs through forest toward the basin, with an unbridged ford of the Chiwawa headwater around 4,400 ft — manageable at summer flow, higher and pushier early. Above the ford the brush thickens and the tread fades: favour the more open, less-timbered ground along the east side of the basin, because drifting into the timber turns this into a bushwhack.

Camp is on benches around 6,300 ft. Several lines reach them: the left-trending gully is the most direct and easiest going though it is wet, and the vegetated slopes beside the talus gullies are the better choice coming down.

FR-6200 has been closed to vehicles beyond Atkinson Flat since May 20, 2026 under storm-damage order 06-17-07-2026-11 (through December 31, 2027), so Trinity is not reachable by vehicle. The Little Giant Fire closure (order 06-17-07-2026-40) also closes the Chiwawa River Road and the trails from Trinity through October 31, 2026 unless lifted sooner.

ways.name: Phelps Creek variant to the col west of the summit
ways.season: Late Jun-Sep, as for the main line
ways.notes:
A less-travelled alternative starts at the Phelps Creek Trailhead rather than Trinity. It bushwhacks to about 5,500 ft and follows a gully to the right of Point 5971 up to the col west of the summit, then takes easy Class 2 ground along the west ridge to the top.

This is the shorter line on paper and the rougher one on the ground: there is no tread on the bushwhack and no camp equivalent to the Chiwawa Basin benches. It is genuinely used, but not recommended over the Trinity approach.

ways.name: Colchuck Lake, snow-covered glacier (early season)
ways.season: Jun-early Jul, while the glacier is well filled and crevasses stay bridged
ways.notes:
Stuart Lake Trail #1599 from the FR 7601 road end for about 2.5 miles to the signed fork, then right onto the Colchuck Lake Trail for another 1.6 miles of steep switchbacks through boulders to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft. Call it four miles and 2,200 ft. This is the last reliable water.

Follow the boot path along the east shore to the inlet at the south end, then leave the trail. Gain the crest of the lateral moraine as early as you can — the alternative is a long session in genuinely loose scree and talus, and parties consistently report an hour of boulder-hopping through it when they stay low.

With good snow cover much of this basin, and later much of the glacier, can be glissaded on the way out, which is why parties favour the early window. Aim to be off the glacier before early afternoon: it softens badly and post-holing plus wet-slide potential make a late descent both slow and unpleasant.

ways.name: Colchuck Lake, bare-ice glacier (late season)
ways.season: Aug-Sep, once the glacier has opened up and gone to bare, sun-cupped ice
ways.notes:
The walk to Colchuck Lake and up the moraine is the same, and easier without snow. What changes is everything above the moraine.

By August the glacier typically melts out to hard, sun-cupped ice. It is not heavily crevassed, but crevasses and marginal moats that were bridged in June are open, and the surface no longer takes a boot step. Crampons and an axe stop being optional and a rope becomes a real consideration for the margins.

The scree and talus below the moraine is at its loosest now, and rockfall off the surrounding walls is more frequent with no snow holding things in place. The glissade descent is gone — plan on down-climbing everything you came up, which is the main reason the day gets longer.

ways.name: Swamp Creek climbers' path to the col
ways.season: Early to mid summer gives firm, well-bridged snow with least crevasse danger; by late summer more crevasses are open and the glacier is less stable.
ways.notes: This is the line most descriptions still call standard, and it is the brushy one. From the road end at the bridge, follow the crest trail south to the first creekside camp and on to the camp at the Swamp Creek fork. Leave the maintained trail there for the long-abandoned climbers' path: cross Swamp Creek on a large log to its east side and force about a quarter mile of dense slide alder and vine maple. Above that a headwall bars the basin; the way up it is at the far left, and the route then climbs steep forest, veering right at the end to a natural saddle around 5,040 ft. Beyond lies a further, higher basin near 5,500 ft below the slabs of the receding glacier.

ways.name: Crest trail to Hemlock Camp and the northwest climb
ways.season: Early to mid summer for the best glacier conditions, and tied to the boat and shuttle timetable at both ends.
ways.notes: The newer variant continues farther south on the crest trail, roughly to the Hemlock camp, then leaves the trail and climbs northwest through open forest and slopes — about 3,500 ft of gain — to reach the glacier from the ridge above. It avoids nearly all of the Swamp Creek brush and is substantially easier ground, even though the Swamp Creek line is still the one usually called standard. It is the better choice for a party that wants to arrive with something left, and it is what the far side of the ridge separating this peak from its neighbour gives access to.

ways.name: Eldorado Creek climbers' path to Inspiration Glacier high camp
ways.season: Jul-Sep, once the talus is bare
ways.notes:
Drive Cascade River Road from Marblemount roughly 20 miles to the Eldorado parking area at about 2,100 ft. The first ten miles are paved; the rest is gravel and washboard.

The path does not leave from the parking area. Walk back down the road about 90 feet and look for the log (historically a large single log, sometimes a clump of trees) spanning the Cascade River. The crossing shifts year to year and is slick when wet — a handline is worth carrying for a party that is not confident on a log. On the far bank walk perpendicular to the river roughly 100 feet to pick up the boot path.

The path climbs steeply and relentlessly through old-growth timber with no water, gaining about 1,500 ft before it breaks out into the boulder field. Follow cairns and flagging up the boulders, staying climber's right so you do not cross Eldorado Creek unnecessarily. The boulder field is universally described as the worst part of the trip, and worse on the way down with a heavy pack.

Above the boulders the ground eases into Eldorado Creek Basin (roughly 5,400-5,600 ft, about 3 miles and 3,300 ft from the car), a common first camp. To continue, climb onto the rocky ridge at about 6,100 ft and drop a few hundred feet on the far side into Roush Creek Basin (6,100-6,400 ft, running water). From Roush, broken talus and slabs lead onto the toe of the Eldorado Glacier; rope up here. Moderate glacier slopes lead to high camp on the Eldorado-Inspiration saddle around 7,500-7,800 ft.

Overnight stays need a North Cascades National Park backcountry permit. Eldorado is a high-use cross-country zone; there is an advance lottery and reservations on Recreation.gov, but permits for the areas off Cascade River Road (Eldorado, Boston Basin, Cascade Pass) must be picked up in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.

ways.name: Late-spring snow cover (skis or boots)
ways.season: late May-June
ways.notes:
In late spring the upper approach is continuous snow and the boulder field problem largely disappears, which is why many parties prefer this window. It does not make the whole approach snow: a late-May park report described the route as snow-free until just before Eldorado Basin was gained around 5,000 ft, with the boulder fields completely melted out — so expect a dry, steep forest climb first and snow only above.

Ski parties commonly carry ski boots and walk the forest section in approach or running shoes, switching over at snow line.

The trade is avalanche exposure. Large avalanches sweep parts of this route in winter and spring, and Cascade River Road itself can be buried by avalanche debris miles below the trailhead in a heavy year, adding road miles before you even start.

ways.name: From the north — Cascade Pass and the glacier corridor
ways.season: Mid-July through September, once the Cache Col snow has consolidated and the Red Ledge is clear of verglas; the whole corridor has to be in condition, not just the peak.
ways.notes: Lizard has no trailhead of its own and is normally met partway through the high traverse rather than approached. From the Cascade River Road end, the maintained trail switchbacks up a forested rib and then traverses meadow and talus to Cascade Pass, which is the last built tread of the trip. Leave it there and work south and east across the Mixup flank on boot path, talus and snow to the Cache Glacier and Cache Col, then drop the steep snow on the far side to the tarn at Kool-Aid Lake. Beyond, the Red Ledge cuts the cliff band west of Art's Knoll, then the Middle Cascade Glacier leads to the Spider-Formidable col and down to Yang Yang Lakes. From there the line climbs past Le Conte Mountain, crosses the Le Conte Glacier to the gap north of Sentinel Peak, and crosses the South Cascade Glacier to the col at its head before dropping into the White Rock Lakes basin. Lizard is the side trip from that camp: climb back out of the basin northeast to the broad notch on the peak's south ridge.

ways.name: From the south — Downey Creek and Bachelor Creek (road closed at milepost 4)
ways.season: Late July through September. The Bachelor Creek brush is worst before the snow has settled it and the Bachelor Creek ford is worst during peak melt.
ways.notes: Not usable while the Suiattle River Road stays closed at milepost 4 under a Forest Service order in effect April 2, 2026 through January 1, 2028 unless rescinded sooner; washouts cut off the Downey Creek Trailhead, and the Forest Service's Miner's Fire order (06-05-26-17) also closes the trailhead and the Downey Creek and Bachelor Creek trails from August 15 through December 31, 2026. Before the closure this was the other end of the same corridor. From the Downey Creek Trailhead on the Suiattle River Road, Downey Creek Trail #768 enters wilderness within the first half mile and climbs gently through old growth, crossing tributary creeks that run high in early season, to the Bachelor Creek junction. The Bachelor Creek path is unmaintained, steadily steeper, and notorious for blowdown, with an alder and slide-alder band around 3,800 to 4,400 ft that becomes a genuine bushwhack when snow has not flattened it. It fords Bachelor Creek itself, which runs fast and cold with snowmelt. Above treeline the tread breaks into meadows near Bachelor Meadows and reaches Cub Lake, reliable water and a common first camp. A steep, often snow-covered pitch gains Itswoot Ridge; from there the route climbs to Spire Col, descends the Dana Glacier to White Rock Lakes, and regains the col on Lizard's south ridge from the lakes.

ways.name: Cathedral Pass and Peggy's Pond, then the east ridge and Lynch draw
ways.season: Jun-mid Jul, while Pea Soup Lake is frozen and the moat closed; the lake crossing gets hard once it melts
ways.notes:
Hike the Cathedral Rock Trail to Nosh Nosh Wahtum (formerly Squaw Lake) at 2.5 miles, continue to Cathedral Pass at 5,550 ft, then turn left (west) onto the PCT. In less than half a mile turn right (northwest) onto Trail #1375 — do not follow the PCT down toward Deep Lake. Follow #1375 past Cathedral Rock to Peggy's Pond at about 5,560 ft and camp there. This is the shorter approach with the longer summit day, and it avoids the brush of the alternative.

From camp, climb to about 6,300 ft on the east ridge, then traverse below the Daniel Glacier at 6,100 to 6,300 ft toward Lynch draw.

Trailhead to camp is about 2.5 to 4 hours; camp to summit 5 to 7 hours.

ways.name: Deception Pass, Marmot and Jade Lakes, and Dip Top Gap from the east
ways.season: Early season, roughly June into July, before the moat opens
ways.notes:
From the Deception Pass trailhead, hike to Marmot and Jade Lakes and continue to Dip Top Gap. From the gap, traverse west to the shoulder overlooking the Foss River drainage, then descend to the outlet of Pea Soup Lake.

This is the longer, eastern line into the same basin. It reaches the Lynch Glacier at the same point the Peggy's Pond approach does, and everything about identifying the ice is identical from the lake outlet onward.

ways.name: Stuart Lake trailhead and the Mountaineer Creek valley to the 5,400 ft basin
ways.season: Roughly Apr-Jun; the ice cliff and the couloir exit get harder and more broken as the season runs on
ways.notes: Start at the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of Eightmile Road, about 3,400 ft. Follow the main trail to the first fork, roughly two and a half to three miles in near 4,600 ft, and stay right for Stuart Lake. Left is Colchuck Lake, a different basin on the other side of the ridge. About a mile to a mile and a half past that junction, the Stuart Lake trail turns uphill and swings right, away from the water, and begins switchbacking. That turn is your cue. Leave the trail there and stay flat in the valley bottom with Mountaineer Creek. The test is simple and works in poor visibility: if you are gaining elevation on switchbacks you are walking to Stuart Lake and you have missed it. Cross Mountaineer Creek on logs. There is no single canonical log and parties describe several sporty crossings that shift with the snowpack; early season, snowbanks make dropping onto a log awkward. On the far side, pick up the climbers' path along the creek. It is unmaintained, full of blowdown and re-routes, and the cairns are not to be trusted: they invite you up and right into a boulder slope around 4,675 ft. Two parties independently say stay low beside the creek instead, with the creek on your left — the path is unpleasant but the better line. Some parties do use the boulder field deliberately to avoid the creek crossings, so treat it as a genuine choice rather than a mistake. After about a mile and a half the valley steepens. Turn right and west and climb talus and forest into a hanging flat basin at about 5,400 ft, under the Sherpa and Ice Cliff glaciers. That right-turn-and-climb out of a steepening valley into flat ground is the arrival cue for the bivy.

ways.name: Early-season approach with the Eightmile road gated
ways.season: Spring, roughly Apr-May, when the route is in as snow and ice
ways.notes:
When Eightmile Road is snowed or gated below the trailhead, add roughly two and a half miles of road before the trail proper. Parties walk that stretch and then put skis on, skinning the Stuart Lake trail, before continuing on foot.

This is a genuinely different day rather than a longer walk: the valley is snow-covered, the log crossings may be buried or may be harder to reach off a snowbank, and the boulder-field-versus-creek question largely disappears under snow. Postholing on the cross-country section is the common complaint.

No reliable published trailhead-to-bivy time exists for either version, so plan from your own pace rather than from a number.

ways.name: Bedal Creek Trail #705 (FR 4096)
ways.season: Jul-Sep, once the forest band below 4,900 ft is clear of snow
ways.notes:
From the Mountain Loop Highway take FR 4096, a rough narrow spur where high clearance genuinely helps, to the Bedal Creek trailhead at about 2,790 ft. Distance and gain above are the full round trip by this line.

Walk the old Bedal Creek trail roughly 1.5 miles and 700 ft. It is overgrown in stretches but stays followable. The critical junction is around 3,500 ft, where a climbers' path turns off to the left near 48.0560, -121.3631; it has carried pink flagging tape in recent years. Missing that turn is the standard error here — the old tread continues and dies in a brushy washout below the basin.

The climbers' path gains about 1,400 ft steeply through forest. At roughly 4,900 ft it breaks out into talus, then bends southeast through meadow and scattered timber to the Bedal-Sloan saddle at 5,300 ft, where a shallow, somewhat stagnant pond marks the usual camp. This is the last easy water; cascading streams just below the saddle are the alternative.

Southeast from the saddle the ground opens into scramble terrain. At about 5,800 ft you cross a minor rock ridge and get your first view of the glacier. Snow from here is often firm in the morning and may want axe and crampons.

ways.name: North Fork Sauk / Cougar Creek (FR 49)
ways.season: Jul-Aug, after the North Fork Sauk drops from snowmelt flow
ways.notes:
The start is an unsigned climbers' pullout on FR 49 (Sloan Creek Road) at roughly 1,900 ft, on the north side of the North Fork Sauk. It is not the maintained North Fork Sauk River Trail #649 — that is a different trailhead a short distance back along the road, and taking it is the common mistake.

The path runs flat and brushy through stinging nettle and then devil's club for a few tenths of a mile before dropping to the river. The river must be forded or crossed on a log jam; jams are usually adequate around half a mile in but shift from year to year and are a poor bet in high water. The path then crosses river braids two or three times over the next mile before turning up Cougar Creek on a faint, intermittently cairned and flagged track through sandy streambed and forest.

Around 3,000-3,200 ft the path crosses Cougar Creek itself; lower crossings can be impassable, so hold out for the 3.2K-ish one. Steep forest switchbacks follow, passing a waterfall on Cougar Creek near 5,000 ft — roughly two to two and a half hours from the car and the last reliable water before the basin. Above the falls the track leaves the trees onto scree and slabs and angles up to the 5,800 ft basin on Sloan's northeast side, where there is a small stream and the standard bivy. This line converges with the Bedal Creek approach around 5,000-5,500 ft.

ways.name: Lower Maynard Burn Trail #816 over Baldy and along the crest
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. North-facing gullies on the last stretch hold steep snow into July
ways.notes:
There is no roadside access to this ridge; the drive only gets you to the trailhead at the end of FR-2860-120, off FR-2870 / Lost Mountain Road, itself off Palo Alto Road south of US-101 near Sequim. Road-end parking at a dirt berm, about 3,300 ft, Northwest Forest Pass required.

Lower Maynard Burn Trail #816 leaves the berm on an old roadbed and crosses Mueller Creek almost immediately — the last easy reliable water for a long stretch, so fill up. The trail narrows to single-track around 0.3 mile and then turns relentlessly steep, gaining roughly 3,000 ft in a little over two miles of fall-line tread with essentially no switchbacks, in places barely a boot-width across eroded crumbly ravine crossings and slopes of packed dirt and shattered shale. It is a climber's path, not a graded trail.

At about 2.7 miles and 6,200 ft it tops out on the saddle between Tyler Peak and Baldy, where a short steep side path drops off the crest to a snowmelt spring — the last dependable water on the route.

ways.name: Royal Basin and the east face, for a traverse rather than an out-and-back
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
ways.notes:
The other end of the same ridge, and the reason to know it is that it turns this route into a traverse instead of a there-and-back over Baldy twice. From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead, the Royal Basin Trail leads to Royal Lake and Upper Royal Basin. From the ridge, the east face drops roughly 3,000 ft to intersect the Royal Basin Trail.

It is steep, loose and only lightly travelled: packed dirt and shattered shale, brushy notches, and picking through timber looking for blazes and cairns. Some parties scree-ski the looser upper sections rather than rope up at all. It is not a bolted or standardised line — where parties do rope down a short cliffy step, anchors are improvised from trees or natural rock horns.

Most commonly this is used as the exit after climbing from Maynard Burn, closing a loop out Royal Basin or back over the ridge.

ways.name: The long way: the ridge trail from the north to a camp near the boundary high point
ways.season: July through September; the gravel road governs the season at its own end
ways.notes:
There is no road to this peak from the south. From the highway on the north side of the boundary, follow the valley road south on gravel through the provincial park to the trailhead - a slow drive of well over an hour. Confirm the boundary gate's status before planning: the crossing at Hozomeen has been closed to both vehicle and foot traffic.

From the trailhead, climb roughly four thousand feet on trail to the ridge junction, then turn south along the ridge over rolling ground to a camp near the boundary high point at about 6,345 ft. Take water from the three creeks in the forest below the ridge, because there is none again until you are well south of the boundary.

ways.name: The short way: the border swath from the ranger station
ways.season: July through September, and slower than its distance suggests
ways.notes: A much shorter start leaves from the ranger station at the head of the lake, follows the short interpretive loop, and then bushwhacks east up the overgrown boundary swath, past a swamp, gaining about three thousand feet to a col near 6,300 ft where it joins the ridge. It saves miles and costs hours - the swath is overgrown rather than cleared, and the ground is steep and brushy. Reaching the ranger station itself means either the water taxi up the lake or the gated road from the north.

ways.name: Canyon Creek trailhead, Crater Lake, and the traverse over the Jerry Glacier
ways.season: Mid-July through September, once the Jerry Glacier crossing is reasonable and before fresh snow lands on the loose face
ways.notes:
From the Canyon Creek Trailhead at about 1,900 ft, cross Canyon Creek and follow Trail #738 as it switchbacks hard through forest - three and a half to four thousand feet of climbing with no water on it, so fill up at the creek. Bear left at the Crater Lake trail junction and contour to the lake basin, then pick the trail back up above the lake for long, hot, exposed switchbacks with nothing to drink on them. Somewhere between 6,700 and 7,200 ft leave the maintained tread and traverse to the gap between Crater Mountain's summit and its east peak at about 7,200 ft. From that saddle the route goes downhill onto the Jerry Glacier: snow-covered and crevassed enough for a rope and crampons early, often patchy or bare late, when a slip runs further. Descend off the ice into the Jerry Lakes basin and fill water - it is the last of it before the face.

Check the Canyon Creek crossing before you commit: it has been described both as a log-and-plank crossing and as a ford with the bridge gone, and it is the first obstacle of the trip.

ways.name: Two camps at the end of the same approach: Jerry Lakes or Crater Creek Meadows
ways.season: Same window; the meadows camp holds water later into the season than snow patches by the lakes
ways.notes: The approach is identical as far as the Jerry Lakes basin and then forks on where you sleep. Camping at the lakes near 6,400 ft is the shorter day in and keeps water at the tent.
