Continuing over the notch just south of the lakes and dropping about six hundred feet into Crater Creek Basin puts camp in meadows near 6,000 ft north-west of Point 7,001 - a longer day in with a re-ascent at the end, but it starts summit day already on the right side of the notch and out of the wind.

ways.name: Blue Lake Trail to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch
ways.season: Jul-Sep (dry)
ways.notes:
Park at the Blue Lake Trailhead on the south side of SR-20, roughly 1 mile west of Washington Pass, at about 5,400 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required and the lot is small enough that it fills on summer weekends.

Walk the maintained Blue Lake Trail for about 1.7 miles. The turnoff is a signed junction — the sign points straight on for Blue Lake and left for Liberty Bell Trail #727, Climbing Access — and it sits just past a small stream in a meadow, with a large cairn beside it. That stream is the last water you can count on.

Trail #727 climbs hard through granite slabs, talus and heather benches toward the gully that drains the notch between Liberty Bell and Concord Tower. In the gully itself the loose ground is least bad if you keep to climber's left for the lower two thirds, then cross and hug climber's right for the rest. Where the boot path forks a couple of hundred feet below the notch, take the left branch; the right branch leads on toward Lexington and Concord's south side.

ways.name: Early-season snow gully to the notch
ways.season: Highway opening (typically mid-late Apr or early May) through late Jun
ways.notes:
The same line as the summer approach, but the upper gully below the Liberty Bell-Concord notch commonly holds snow into late June and the boot path through the slabs and heather may be buried lower down. Parties carry an ice axe, and crampons if the snow has refrozen overnight.

SR-20 over Washington and Rainy Passes is gated every winter — it typically closes in late November or early December and reopens somewhere between mid-April and early May, with the exact dates set by snowpack and avalanche conditions rather than a calendar. Until the gate opens there is no drive-up access to the Blue Lake Trailhead at all.

ways.name: Eagle Lakes Trail #431 to Upper Eagle Lake
ways.season: Roughly July through October, once road and trail are snow-free. Snow lingers in the notch through the lower cliff band into summer and makes the route-finding harder.
ways.notes: From the road-end trailhead at the top of the forest-road spur, fill out the self-issue wilderness permit and start up Eagle Lakes Trail #431. The tread crosses Crater Creek on a bridge early on — stay straight where the Crater Creek Trail splits — and climbs steadily, with an established camp roughly halfway. Past an overlook of the lower lake the trail reaches a junction: the left branch goes to the lower lake and the pass beyond, the right-hand spur climbs a half mile to Upper Eagle Lake. Take the spur. The upper lake sits in a cirque with established campsites and is the last reliable water and the staging point before the off-trail push, which starts from its northwest shore.

ways.name: Horsehead Pass and the west slopes
ways.season: July through October. The west side melts out and stays passable later in the autumn than the shaded notch on the east side.
ways.notes: The easier alternative stays on the main trail past the Upper Eagle Lake spur, continues to the lower lake and climbs to Horsehead Pass, then gains the peak's west slopes from the far side of the crest. It trades the exposed scrambling for distance and a long, loose walk-up, and is the sensible choice for a party that does not want the cliff-band route-finding or that finds snow still lying in the notch above the upper lake.

ways.name: Dosewallips roadbed, Lake Constance trail, Avalanche Canyon and the South Chute
ways.season: Jun-Sep; June snow makes the South Chute far pleasanter than late-summer scree
ways.notes:
Park at the Dosewallips road washout around 600 ft, reached from US 101 at Brinnon on FR 2610. The road has been closed to vehicles since a washout in 2002, so the first 5 miles up the Dosewallips valley are on the old roadbed.

The Lake Constance climbers' path is signed but unmaintained and carries no Forest Service trail number — it is a boot path. It launches straight into root-and-branch pulling through old burn debris for the first 0.4 mile before the old growth closes in. At about 0.8 mile, Half Acre Rock is a large monolith with campsites beside Constance Creek and is the obvious rest and water stop; by late summer the creek and the canyon above it run dry, so treat it as the last reliable water below the lake.

Past 1.1 miles the brush opens onto steep exposed slopes, and by 1.3 miles the creek is forced through a defile and the path is pushed up and over a series of rock ledges and short cliff bands, using roots and a landmark Alaska cedar to gain the next ledge. Exposure increases with each one and a slip is serious.

All told it gains roughly 3,200-3,400 ft in under two miles to Lake Constance at 4,680-4,800 ft, one of the steepest approach trails in the Olympics. Lake Constance is a reservable Olympic National Park backcountry site with reservations for the May 15-October 15 summer season; a wilderness permit is required for the overnight, and parties of seven or more must use the designated group sites.

ways.name: Bike the closed Dosewallips roadbed
ways.season: Jun-Sep
ways.notes:
The roughly 5 miles of closed roadbed between the washout and the Lake Constance path is old road surface rather than trail, and mountain-biking it is a common way to cut the walk at both ends of the trip. The bike is left at the signed start of the climbers' path.

Everything above that point is identical to the walk-in variant: the same unmaintained boot path, the same 3,200-3,400 ft in under two miles, the same rock ledges and the same lake.

The same permit rules apply — a wilderness permit for the overnight at Lake Constance, reservable for the May 15-October 15 summer season, with group sites required for parties of seven or more.

ways.name: Rainy Pass, the crest trail to Methow Pass, and the east ridge
ways.season: Late June through September, with July through September giving the driest scree. June ascents work but the final slopes and gully still hold snow and want an axe and crampons. The highway is shut for avalanche control through the winter, which closes both approaches outright.
ways.notes: The long way, and the one that suits a two-day trip. From the large paved lot on the north side of SR-20 at Rainy Pass, follow the crest trail north as it climbs steadily through subalpine forest and larch parkland past Porcupine Creek — fill up there, it is the last easy water before a long dry stretch of switchbacks — to Cutthroat Pass. From the pass the trail drops toward Granite Pass and a saddle beyond it, where a steep snowfield often lasts into August and has caused slide-for-life falls, so carry an axe if you are early in the season. Beyond, the trail contours across open, sparsely treed slopes to Snowy Creek Meadow, a common water and camp stop, with a short side trail west into the Snowy Lakes basin for a higher and more scenic bivy under Tower Mountain and Golden Horn. From the meadow, stay on the crest trail north to the open plateau at Methow Pass and leave it there: travel west and southwest off-trail through open heather and talus benches toward the peak's east ridge, gain the ridge, and follow moderate sand, scree and talus — loose in places, with real route-finding — up to the saddle between the true summit and its lower false summit.

ways.name: Swamp Creek pullout and the south ridge
ways.season: Late June through September once the snow finger has stabilised or melted, with July and August driest. Earlier in the season the finger is a snow climb rather than a scramble.
ways.notes: The short, steep alternative, and the way most day parties go. Start from the highway pullout at Swamp Creek and climb through brushy forest to the foot of the prominent ridge on the mountain's south side. Follow the ridge upward, staying on the crest where it lets you and moving climber's right to get around the cliff bands that block the crest around 5,200 ft — getting that traverse wrong is what turns parties back. Above the cliff bands the ridge opens out onto sand and scree and continues to the summit block. This side faces the sun and dries early, which is why it comes into condition before the crest-trail approach and why it turns into a loose, dusty grind by late summer; a snow finger on this flank can hold firm snow at a fairly steep angle into early summer, which speeds the ascent considerably for a party carrying an axe.

ways.name: White Salmon Creek roadbed, then the ridgecrest opposite the ski area
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. This is the more direct of the two options and it is a bushwhack, so it wants the ground clear rather than snow-covered
ways.notes:
Park at the lower White Salmon lodge on SR-542 (White Salmon Road, FR-3075) and follow the dirt road up the White Salmon Creek drainage for under a mile. This first stretch is common to both options.

The direct option then drops off-trail across White Salmon Creek and climbs to the ridgecrest directly opposite the ski area, then follows that crest to the base of the mountain's north side.

This is a long Cascade adventure route rather than a line with a bootpack: bushwhacking, complex route-finding, runout and loose rock, moderate alpine ice, and extensive glacier travel, all in one day.

ways.name: Up the White Salmon valley to the lower glacier, then onto the crest
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
ways.notes:
The alternative from the same parking: continue up the road as far as it goes, then travel off-trail up the valley until open slopes allow access to the lower White Salmon Glacier, and gain the crest of the arête from there.

It trades the creek crossing and the direct climb to the crest for more valley travel and a glacier approach. Parties choosing between the two are choosing between bushwhack-then-ridge and valley-then-glacier; both are documented and neither is a shortcut.

ways.name: Depot Creek from the north side of the border to the lake camp
ways.season: Late July through September, for a crossable glacier and a passable creek
ways.notes:
From the road washout at about 2,600 ft, reached by a rough spur off the lake road on the Canadian side, walk the old roadbed about nine minutes to an inconspicuous spur on the left, follow that spur four minutes to a T-junction, and bear right onto an extremely overgrown and sporadically muddy road for about thirty-five minutes. That brings you to the boundary obelisk, where there is a register - carry a passport, because this approach crosses the international border on foot.

Above the boundary the way becomes a crude but discernible climbers' path along the creek through old growth, easy where deadfall has been cut and full of uncut logs where it has not. About three miles in it reaches the falls, which are the real crux of the approach: wet slick boulders and slabs at their base, with steep steps rigged with an old fixed hand-line. Treat the line as an aid rather than as protection, and back it up with a heavy pack on.

Above the falls the path continues through meadow and upper valley to the lake at roughly 5,700 ft - flat sandy mostly treeless benches at the toe of the talus, the standard base camp for this peak and its neighbour, with reliable water.

ways.name: From Ross Lake by boat and up Silver Creek to the lake basin
ways.season: Late July through September, once the boat is running and the cross-country is clear of snow
ways.notes:
The other side of the mountain is reached without leaving the United States. A booked water taxi runs a long way up Ross Lake to a drop at the mouth of Silver Creek at about 1,600 ft. A trail climbs the north side of the creek for roughly two and a half miles to an old cabin at about 2,900 ft, above which the way is cross-country with occasional blazes across slide alder and forest slopes to the camp in the Silver Lake basin at about 6,763 ft.

This puts you on the opposite side of the peak from the Depot Creek camp, so it changes which col you reach and in what order - plan the climb from this camp rather than translating a description written from the other one.

ways.name: Longs Pass from Esmeralda TH — summer scramble
ways.season: Jul-Sep, once the couloir has melted to talus
ways.notes: Drive the North Fork Teanaway River Road (FR 9737) to the Esmeralda Basin road-end parking at about 4,243 ft. A quarter mile of old mining road leads to a fork; take the right branch for Longs Pass. The trail climbs an open, south-facing hillside with essentially no shade — in July and August this is a pre-dawn start, not a preference. Longs Pass sits around 6,200-6,250 ft, roughly 2,000 ft above the car in about two miles, and it is the single most useful place on the whole approach. From the pass, drop the steep loose scree on the north side, losing 1,200-1,400 ft to Ingalls Creek at about 4,800 ft. Cross the creek — there is a summer log crossing, and in high melt it is worth walking to find it rather than wading — then follow the Ingalls Creek Trail upvalley (west) a short way to the meadow and camps below the couloir's outlet. Good camps sit on the valley floor more or less straight south of where the couloir comes down, with a few more near the footlog. From camp a climbers' path threads the meadow to the toe of the couloir. This is also the standard descent for the North Ridge, West Ridge and most of the rest of Stuart, so expect to share it.

ways.name: Longs Pass from Esmeralda TH — spring snow climb
ways.season: May-Jun as a snow route; road access is the limiting factor earlier
ways.notes:
The same line, in a completely different medium. With the couloir snow-filled it is a straightforward steep snow climb rather than a scree grind, and many parties prefer it this way — but it demands axe and crampons, an early start, and a hard turnaround, because the whole thing faces south and softens fast.

FR 9737 is a gravel road that is not maintained through winter and is generally not clear until late June in a heavy year, so a genuinely early-season attempt means adding road miles on foot or ski. Check the road before committing.

The Longs Pass hillside carries avalanche exposure in winter and spring conditions, and the north-side drop to Ingalls Creek holds snow that can be firm and icy at dawn and slushy by mid-morning.

ways.name: Blue Lake Trail and the Concord-Lexington gully
ways.season: Jul-Sep
ways.notes:
Start at the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft) on SR-20 just under a mile west of Washington Pass. Follow the maintained Blue Lake Trail until the terrain opens up — around a mile and a half to two miles — and pick up the well-established climbers' path branching left at a large cairn.

From there, leave the line most parties take toward the Liberty Bell-Concord notch and work up into the next gully south, the one that separates Lexington Tower from Concord Tower. As you gain height in that gully a decent boot path shows up along its left side; use it. It brings you to the Concord-Lexington col.

Carry water from the trailhead. Snowmelt trickles low in the basin dry up by mid-summer.

ways.name: Early-season snow to the Concord-Lexington col
ways.season: Highway opening through late Jun
ways.notes:
Same approach, but the upper gully to the col commonly holds firm snow into early summer, which buries the boot path along its left side and turns the last stretch into a snow climb. Carry an axe, and crampons if it is refrozen.

SR-20 is gated across Washington Pass through the winter — typically closing in late November or early December and reopening between mid-April and early May — so there is no drive-up access until the highway reopens.

ways.name: Aasgard Pass to the Core, dry conditions
ways.season: late Jul-Sep, once Aasgard Pass is bare talus
ways.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead, left onto the Colchuck Lake Trail at the signed junction, and about four miles and 2,200 ft to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft. Filter here; there is nothing simple above until the Core.

Skirt the east and south shore to the boulder field at the lake's south end and start up Aasgard Pass: roughly 2,000-2,200 ft in under a mile, on what regulars fairly describe as a jenga pile. Follow the outlet drainage and stay climber's left (east) of the first band of cliffs. Veering climber's right toward the waterfall complex on Colchuck Peak's flank is the classic and repeatedly fatal error here — people have died on that side and it cliffs out easily. Near the top the path passes in front of a small waterfall and climbs steeply beside a much larger one; missing the turn there puts you on vertical rock.

Cairns are everywhere on Aasgard and they mark more than one line. Trust the worn tread over the cairn.

Top out around 7,800-7,841 ft, then lose 600-700 ft east through the Core's tarns and slabs, then climb north to Prusik Pass. In the Core there are a couple of places where it is easy to add distance without adding progress, but the navigation is not hard in clear weather.

Most parties do this car-to-car, and a fit team should expect a 20-21 hour day; the Enchantments overnight permit lottery is competitive enough that camping is not a plan you can rely on.

ways.name: Aasgard Pass with snow, early season
ways.season: May-early Jul, while the pass holds continuous snow
ways.notes:
Same line, different problem. With snow on it, Aasgard is an axe-and-sometimes-crampons proposition rather than a talus grind, and it is avalanche terrain in shoulder season.

Early-season snow softens through the day into deep, punchy stuff that hides ice underneath, and the hidden creek running beneath the talus is a real hazard where snow bridges it. The consolidated dawn snow that makes the ascent quick is also the surface that makes an uncontrolled slide easy.

On the plus side the route-finding is simpler with the talus buried, and the Core beyond the pass travels fast on snow.

On the north side of Prusik itself, snow adds both hazard and time to the rappel descent — budget for it.

ways.name: Snow Lakes and the lower Enchantments to Prusik Pass
ways.notes: From the Snow Lakes Trailhead, climb past Snow Lakes and Lake Viviane to the Gnome Tarn and Prusik Pass area below the peak. More gain than Aasgard Pass but no steep snow or talus headwall.

ways.name: Boston Basin to the SE Ridge notch — early season, snow gully
ways.season: Jun-mid Jul, while the approach gully still holds snow
ways.notes:
Same start as everything else in Boston Basin: the unsigned pullout on Cascade River Road about 21.7 miles from Marblemount at roughly 3,200-3,300 ft, the old Diamond Mine roadbed for about three quarters of a mile, then the sharp right onto the steep climbers' trail. Four stream crossings, then treeline at about 5,300 ft. Low camp on heather benches at 5,300-5,700 ft, higher camp on the knoll at about 6,300-6,400 ft.

From camp, skirt climber's left of the Quien Sabe Glacier and gain it relatively high, then rope up and traverse east/climber's right along the top of the glacier several hundred feet until you are directly beneath the tower.

Early season the approach gully is snow, around 35 degrees, and is the pleasant version of this approach — crampons and an axe, straightforward booting. A bergschrund or seracs can bar the direct entry; class 3-4 slabs on the left provide an alternate way in that rejoins the gully about a hundred feet up.

Do the identification work on the walk in, not at the base. The whole sequence — glacier, gully, terrace and notch — is visible from the lower Boston Basin trail and from camp. Look at it in good light while you still have perspective on it.

ways.name: Boston Basin to the SE Ridge notch — late season, dry gully
ways.season: Aug-Sep, once the gully has melted out
ways.notes:
The walk in is identical. What changes is the gully: by late summer the snow is gone and it is loose scree and rubble, manageable but tedious and much more prone to knocking rock onto whoever is below. Trekking poles replace crampons.

The other late-season change is the moat where the glacier meets rock at the gully's base, which opens up as the season goes on and can require a committing step or a short awkward move onto rock.

One recorded late-season day trip left town at 4am, was in Boston Basin by about 8:30am, traversed underneath the tower to find the approach gully, and reached the notch before 11am.

ways.name: Pyramid Lake trail and the Pyramid Peak east ridge to the Colonial Glacier moraine camp
ways.season: Mid-July through September, once the climbers' path is clear of snow and the glacier bridges are still sound
ways.notes:
From the signed gravel pullout on the north side of the highway near milepost 126.8 at about 1,150 ft, the maintained trail climbs steadily through old growth. Rock-hop the creek at roughly a mile - that crossing and the lake are the last easy water for several hours. At the lake, camping is prohibited, so it is a water stop only.

Leave the maintained trail on the lake's south, right-hand side and pick up the unmaintained climbers' path. It is steep and brushy from the first steps and gains roughly two thousand feet in switchbacks onto Pyramid Peak's east ridge, then follows a narrow knolly crest with loose rock and short route-finding steps. Short of Pyramid Peak itself, do not climb it: drop slightly and traverse, often on lingering snow, to the terminal moraine and meltwater tarn at the foot of the Colonial Glacier. The moraine benches are the standard first camp and the tarn is the water. An overnight in the park needs a wilderness permit picked up on the way through.

ways.name: Carrying through to the col camp above the Colonial Glacier
ways.season: Same window; only worth the extra carry once the glacier is reasonable
ways.notes:
Instead of stopping at the moraine, some parties carry over the Colonial Glacier and camp at the broad col near 6,840 ft, where a stream supplies water. It costs a roped carry with overnight loads and puts the tent on an exposed saddle, and it buys a much shorter summit day: the Neve crossing begins immediately from camp rather than after a glacier climb.

The judgement is about weather rather than fitness. The col camp is committing in poor visibility, because the crossing beyond it has no landmarks; the moraine camp keeps you below the ice with an easy retreat.

ways.name: Andrews Creek trail #504 from the Chewuch River road
ways.season: Roughly July through the first snow of October
ways.notes:
The drive is the easy part — paved the whole way from Winthrop up the Chewuch River valley to the Andrews Creek trailhead at about 3,050 ft. The walk is one of the longest wilderness approaches in the state.

Trail #504 climbs the drainage for roughly twelve miles to Andrews Pass above 6,680 ft, crossing an old burn for much of that: hot, rocky, buggy, and no shade. From the pass the trail drops into the next drainage before the Cathedral Lakes side trail climbs to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft, below the peak's south-west side.

Treat this as a two-to-four day backpack with a summit push from camp in the basin. A free self-issue wilderness permit is taken at the trailhead along with a parking pass. There is no cell coverage anywhere on this trip.

ways.name: Cathedral Driveway trail #510A from Loomis via Toats Coulee
ways.season: Roughly July through the first snow of October
ways.notes:
The high trailhead above Loomis, reached by Toats Coulee Road and the forest roads beyond it, sits at about 5,570 ft. This is a trail and not a four-wheel-drive road, whatever you may have read; the high-clearance warning in circulation belongs to a different spur.

The trail drops from the trailhead to meet the valley trail lower down, then follows the valley up to the Cathedral Lakes basin. It is the shortest walk and the least total climbing of the ways in.

Both ends carry a penalty. The drive is about two hours longer than from Winthrop, and because the trailhead is high and the trail loses height to reach the valley, the trip finishes with roughly 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out.

ways.name: Thirtymile Trailhead and the Chewuch River trail toward Remmel Lake
ways.notes: Follow the Chewuch River trail north from the Thirtymile Trailhead nearly to Remmel Lake, then climb to the Cathedral Lakes basin. A longer way round than Andrews Creek, used when combining the Remmel Lake country with the climb.

ways.name: The northern line: Access Creek and Luna Col, then the high traverse over Luna, East Fury and West Fury to the Swiss-Fury saddle
ways.season: Jul-Sep
ways.notes:
From the Ross Dam Trailhead at milepost 134 on WA-20, about a mile of trail and service road drops to Ross Lake, crossed by the resort water taxi or by paddling or walking round. Pick up the Big Beaver Trail north along the lake and follow it roughly 10 miles to Luna Camp, then about 1.5 miles further to the Access Creek drainage.

Leave the trail and climb the brushy, moderately steep Access Creek valley, staying on its north side, to the open basin east of Luna Peak at about 4,300 ft. This is described as the easiest and least brushy approach on the east side of the Pickets. From there, gain Access Col and traverse cross-country and glaciated terrain over Luna Peak, East Fury and West Fury to reach the Swiss-Fury saddle.

ways.name: The southern line: Bacon Creek Road, Porkbelly and Mystery Ridges, Jasper Pass and Crowder's northeast ridge to Pickell Pass
ways.season: Jul-Sep
ways.notes:
The alternate, and the shorter of the two in spirit if not in effort. It reaches Swiss from the south via Bacon Creek Road, Porkbelly Ridge, Mystery Ridge, Jasper Pass, Pioneer Ridge and Mount Crowder's northeast ridge, down to a camp at Pickell Pass.

This line is off-trail for most of its length, so treat the ridge sequence as the route rather than any particular tread.

ways.name: Tupso Pass trailhead, Trail #641 (road drivable)
ways.season: Jul-Oct
ways.notes:
Trail #641 from the Tupso Pass trailhead at the end of FR 41. Forest to Saddle Lake at about two and a half miles — the last easy water, with no fires and no camping within two hundred feet of the shore beyond this point — then up through meadows to Goat Flats at roughly four and a half miles, which has the best camping on the route and views out to Puget Sound.

From Goat Flats the trail climbs about two more miles to Tin Can Gap at roughly six miles, banking most of the day's gain. That is the effective end of the maintained trail and where most walkers turn back.

The trail has been maintained by volunteers in recent years, with large numbers of logs cleared; note that a big fallen log above Saddle Lake has rerouted the tread, and there is a rough connector going straight up and down to the next switchback.

ways.name: Road-closure variation — walk or bike FR 41
ways.season: whenever the road is closed at the washout
ways.notes:
FR 41 is closed to vehicles at the washed-out Canyon Creek bridge, leaving roughly nine miles of road between the closure and the trailhead. Vehicles are barred past the barrier but foot and bike traffic are allowed, and biking the road is the common tactic.

Treat this as a standing possibility rather than a one-off: check with the Darrington Ranger District or the Verlot Public Service Center before committing, because the difference is a day hike versus an overnight. There is now a sign at the road marking the old trailhead.

ways.name: Rainy Pass PCT lot, then cross-country east into the meadow basin and the col toward Cutthroat's southwest peak
ways.season: Jul-Oct
ways.notes:
Park at the marked Pacific Crest Trail North trailhead lot on the north side of Rainy Pass at about 4,850 ft, next to the Road 600 turnoff. Leave the PCT almost immediately and strike out cross-country east into open forest, gaining steeply through timber and over downed logs. There is no maintained tread once you leave the PCT.

This is Whistler Mountain above Rainy Pass in Chelan County, not the Whistler Canyon trailhead area near Oroville, which is about 100 miles away and unrelated.

Round trip runs roughly 3.7 miles with about 3,000 ft of gain.

ways.name: The unmarked SR-20 turnout, then a boot path onto the true south ridge at 6,180 ft
ways.season: Jul-Oct
ways.notes:
The second option, and the one that reaches the true south ridge. From the unmarked pullout on SR-20 about 3.1 miles east of Rainy Pass, 0.7 mile before the Blue Lake trailhead, at about 5,000 ft, walk back down and along the road shoulder to a boot path that starts at the west edge of a stand of trees.

About 4 miles round trip with roughly 3,000 ft of gain, the same as the PCT option.

ways.name: Burgundy Col in a single push
ways.season: Jul-Sep
ways.notes:
Park at the pullout on SR-20 near milepost 166, roughly four miles east of Washington Pass and looking straight across the valley at Silver Star Mountain. There is no numbered Forest Service trail here — the whole thing is an established boot path.

Scramble down the embankment past cairns. The first stretch is loose, scree-covered talus before it settles into a proper path. Cross Early Winters Creek on one of the logs; the logjam shifts year to year, so look up and down stream for the best one, and expect a cold, pushy ford in early season.

On the far bank the path winds through forest for about a quarter of a mile, then turns straight uphill between two small creeks and climbs relentlessly. At about 6,460 ft the angle relents at a broad flat bench — big enough for a dozen tents and the obvious rest stop.

Above the bench the path climbs and traverses loose scree gullies before a final cairned stretch of very unstable scree over slab to Burgundy Col at about 7,770 ft, the notch between Burgundy Spire and Paisano Pinnacle. That is roughly 3,700 ft above the creek. That last scree is worse on the way down than the way up.

ways.name: Camp at the 6,460 ft bench
ways.season: Jul-Sep
ways.notes:
The usual way this is done. Walk the same line from the milepost 166 pullout — down the loose talus embankment, across Early Winters Creek on logs, through the forest and then steeply up between the two small creeks — and stop at the broad flat bench at about 6,460 ft, which holds a dozen or more tents and is the natural halfway point. There is usually a seasonal trickle or snowmelt nearby.

Next morning you carry only what you need for the col and the route, which makes the loose scree above the bench substantially less unpleasant. Reckon on the bench being the last flat ground and the last reliable water.

ways.name: Andrews Creek trail #504 from the Chewuch River road
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; snow lingers at Andrews Pass into early July
ways.notes:
Drive north from Winthrop up the Chewuch River road to the Andrews Creek trailhead at about 3,080 ft, roughly a five-hour drive from Seattle and the shortest drive of the three ways in.

Walk Andrews Creek trail #504 up the drainage. The lower miles pass through an old burn, so there is little shade and the tread can be overgrown and wet after rain, but the creek is beside you and reliable. The trail tops out at Andrews Pass above 6,680 ft, where the burn gives way to open parkland.

Continue on the Boundary Trail #533 and drop on the Cathedral Lakes side trail to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft. Published figures for the whole walk from this trailhead are about nineteen miles with 5,550 ft of gain, and everyone splits it over at least two days.

Of the three trailheads this one has the shortest drive and the most walking gain; the Thirtymile trailhead is only about five and a half miles further along the same road, which makes a car shuttle between them easy.

One thing to leave alone: there is a shorter-looking approach from the Canadian side. Crossing into the United States here is illegal, the border is patrolled, and the fines are severe.

ways.name: Cathedral Driveway trail #510A from Loomis via Toats Coulee
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
ways.notes:
This is a trail, #510A, and not a four-wheel-drive road, despite a persistent claim to the contrary — the high-clearance warning in circulation belongs to the Iron Gate spur, a different road. Access is from Loomis by Toats Coulee Road, then a Y junction, then NF-39 and NF-300 to the trailhead at about 5,570 ft.

Be careful with the trailhead name. It appears in print as Cathedral Driveway, Chewuch, and Chewack Driveway, and the Chewuch name also belongs to a completely different trailhead near Winthrop. Navigate to the road, not the name.

The Cathedral Driveway descends from its trailhead to join the Chewuch trail #510 around mile 4.8 at about 4,300 ft, and from there it is the Chewuch valley to the Cathedral Lakes basin. Total is about seventeen and a half miles with roughly 3,700 ft of gain — the shortest walk and the least climbing of the three approaches.

The catch is at both ends. The drive is about two hours longer than from Winthrop, and because the trailhead sits high and the trail drops to meet the Chewuch, you finish the trip with roughly 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out, at the point when you least want it.

ways.name: Thirtymile Trailhead and the Chewuch River trail toward Remmel Lake
ways.notes: Follow the Chewuch River trail north from the Thirtymile Trailhead nearly to Remmel Lake, then climb to the Cathedral Lakes basin. A longer way round than Andrews Creek, used when combining the Remmel Lake country with the climb.

ways.name: Source Lake basin to the divide (summer and fall rock)
ways.season: Jul-Oct, snow-free
ways.notes: Upper Alpental lot, I-90 exit 52. Snow Lake Trail up the valley — the first stretch is the old ski-area cat track — to the fork at about 1.5 miles, then left/west toward Source Lake, where the maintained trail ends near 3,700-3,740 ft. Leave the tread and head northwest into the basin below Chair's east face on climbers' path, talus and heather. The Thumb Tack, a freestanding rock in the basin, is the landmark to aim for; parties commonly reach it in about two hours from the car. At the Thumb Tack there is a genuine fork in what you do next. Continuing up the basin takes you to the foot of the east face. For the Northeast Buttress, angle sharply right from the Thumb Tack and scramble rocky heather slopes and ledges to the top of the divide, then walk along the north side of the divide to the base of the buttress. That line is less obvious than the gully but easier and less exposed.

ways.name: Winter and spring, on snow
ways.season: Dec-Apr, ice and mixed
ways.notes: Same line up the valley, but in snow the summer tread is abandoned and parties skin or boot the valley bottom to Source Lake, then up into the basin, commonly reaching the Thumb Tack shortly after first light. Skis are cached in the basin. In snow the approach gully from the basin up toward the buttress is itself the hazard: it is a classic early-season slide path, and trip reports from this basin describe deep postholing, wet-slab activity and wind loading. Rope, axe and crampons usually come out from the basin onward rather than at the base of the route, because the approach gully is exposed enough on its own.

ways.name: Hannegan Pass and the Chilliwack River Trail to Bear Creek
ways.season: Late July through September, for dry rock and a river crossing that is passable
ways.notes:
From the road end at about 3,100 ft, Trail #674 climbs to Hannegan Pass near 5,100 ft, then drops off the east side into the Chilliwack valley, bearing right at the park boundary onto the Chilliwack River Trail. Past a backcountry camp the trail reaches the Chilliwack River crossing, where a hand-pulled cable car carries hikers over in high water (by late July and August the river is often below knee deep and can be forded), then continues down-valley to the Bear Creek confluence, where the maintained trail ends. The camp there has been closed since the 2021 fire.

Ford Bear Creek, climb steep brushy timber east through huckleberry and slide alder into meadows above Ruta Lake, then traverse the divide - loose south-facing slopes below two unnamed points, and a rock rib - to the broad 6,480 ft saddle with running water and heather tent sites. Two days for most parties.

ways.name: From the Chilliwack Lake road on the Canadian side
ways.season: Same window, and only if the border crossing is confirmed lawful
ways.notes: A much shorter walk to the same saddle camp exists from the road on the Canadian side, but it crosses the border on foot where there is no port of entry, and follows an unmaintained, heavily overgrown tread after the first stretch. It is the natural choice for parties already north of the border and the awkward one for parties starting south of it.

ways.name: South face couloir to the West Ridge notch
ways.season: Jun–early Aug, while it still holds snow
ways.notes: From the Boston Basin high camp, traverse up and east across talus and the remains of the Quien Sabe Glacier toward Forbidden's south face. Where the glacier is melted out, a class 3 rock spur on climber's right is usually faster and drier than staying on snow; where it is snow-covered or crevassed, rope up. The couloir itself runs about 500 ft and steepens to 40–50° near the top, which is where crampons and an axe stop being optional. Reaching the notch is roughly 2,000 ft above camp.

ways.name: Cat Scratch gullies (late season, once the couloir has melted out)
ways.season: Late Aug–Sep, dry conditions
ways.notes: When the couloir has gone to loose talus and scree, the usual line moves off the snow onto the rock gully system immediately west — climber's left — of it. Roughly the first 200 ft is class 4, easing to grassy class 3 for the last 200 ft to the notch. It is loose the whole way, and it is slower than it looks on the approach.

ways.name: Up the gully to its own ledge
ways.notes: From the pullout near milepost 166, hike the gully below the wall for about an hour and follow a narrow ledge back right to the start, a prominent left-arching wide corner. The direct way, and the most practical when the gully is in shape.

ways.name: Via the centre route's lower pitches
ways.season: Summer, once the wall has dried; the pitches used to reach it are the same ones that seep into early summer in wet years.
ways.notes: You can scramble on up the gully to this climb's own ledge, but many parties add pitches instead: do the usual gully approach from the pullout near milepost 166 to the wall's upper ledge, then climb the lower pitches of the centre eleven-pitch line to the shared midway ledge system and traverse left from there. Rack for the pitches you are climbing to get there as well as for this route.

ways.name: Via the right-hand cave route's lower pitches
ways.season: Summer, once the wall has dried.
ways.notes: The same idea from the other side: climb the lower pitches of the right-hand cave line off the upper ledge to reach the shared midway ledge system, then traverse left. This is the longer leftward traverse of the two, so allow for it.

ways.name: Barclay Creek climbers' path — summer line
ways.season: June to September. Early June parties meet significant lingering snow and heavy brush; late July through August is typically the clearest.
ways.notes: From the Barclay Lake trailhead, do not take the maintained lake trail. Walk back down the access road about a quarter mile and pick up the old deactivated spur road — parties who know it often park at the spur's gated start instead of the main lot. Follow the old roadbed a hundred or two hundred yards to a fire-pit clearing, turn right, and pick up the unmarked but well-trodden climbers' path. It drops to the creek and crosses on a log jam or by rock-hopping near the downstream tip of a small mid-channel island; this crossing is the main early-season hazard. On the far bank the path swings west, then north, and starts climbing in earnest through sustained tight switchbacks in second-growth timber. Two decision points follow. Around thirty-six to thirty-eight hundred feet the path forks near a band of exposed rock — stay right and do not scramble the outcrop straight ahead, which is a known trap; the correct line keeps traversing climber's-left beneath a cliff band. Then around forty-four hundred feet the summer line bends left up a brushy weakness in the cliff band rather than continuing up the couloir, which holds snow late. Huckleberry and heather meadows lead to the saddle at about fifty-four hundred feet, the last reliable water.

ways.name: Tailgunner couloir — snow-season line
ways.season: Late spring, while the couloir holds continuous consolidated snow. Once it starts melting out it becomes the wrong answer and the summer line through the brushy weakness is correct.
ways.notes: The same start — the spur road, the fire-pit clearing, the creek crossing at the island, and the switchbacks up through the timber. The difference comes at about forty-four hundred feet: instead of bending left into the brushy weakness in the cliff band, the snow-season line continues directly up the couloir to the saddle. This same couloir is a documented wrong turn in summer and an avalanche path, so it is only reasonable when it is a continuous snow climb and conditions have been assessed.

ways.name: Little Giant Trail #1518 over the pass and down into the Napeequa
ways.season: Jul-Sep, August most reliable. The Chiwawa ford at the very start of this trail is waist-deep and swift in early season and is only reliably safe in late-summer and autumn low water
ways.notes:
The Little Giant Trailhead sits at about 2,600 ft roughly mile 19 of Chiwawa River Road, three miles down-valley of Trinity. The trail begins with an unbridged ford of the Chiwawa River, right at the start — there is no way around it and it is the gate on the whole approach.

Trail #1518 then climbs steeply and badly-eroded to Little Giant Pass at 6,463 ft, with a small spring a few hundred feet below the pass at about 6,250 ft that is the last dependable water before the high basins. Maintained tread effectively ends at the pass.

From the pass the route drops toward the Louis Creek and Napeequa basin, then follows a climbers' path upstream to the end of tread at the creek draining Berge's south-west side. A steep, intermittent boot track climbs through timber to treeline and opens into the south-west basin. A narrow notch at about 7,840 ft in the ridge crest links the Louis Creek basin to the Buck Creek and High Pass side beneath the south-west face, and gaining it is exposed scrambling.

All options to this peak are 15-plus miles round trip and are multi-day trips.

ways.name: Trinity and Buck Creek, or the High Pass high route from Buck Creek Pass
ways.season: Jul-Sep, August most reliable
ways.notes:
Two other ways reach the same mountain from the Trinity side.

The east approach: from Trinity, follow Chiwawa River Trail #1550 about two miles to the Buck Creek Trail #1513 junction, then Buck Creek Trail roughly four to five miles into the basin Berge shares with Mount Cleator and Buck Mountain on its east side.

The north approach: continue past the Buck Creek junction to Buck Creek Pass, then take the climbers' path over High Pass and contour south under Berge's north side near Point 7839. This is the longest by mileage and has the least off-trail travel, which is the trade it offers.

Both involve unbridged or damaged creek crossings and both are multi-day. FR-6200 has been closed beyond Atkinson Flat under a storm-damage order, which affects the drive to Trinity.

ways.name: Phelps Creek and Leroy Basin to the Seven Fingered Jack / Maude col
ways.season: Best while the face still holds continuous snow and ice, roughly Jun into mid-Jul; it used to hold year round and no longer does
ways.notes: Drive the Chiwawa River Road, FR 62, roughly twenty-two miles and turn right onto the Phelps Creek road, FR 6211, to the trailhead at about 3,500 ft. The trail up the valley is the same tread hikers use for Spider Meadow. Walk the Phelps Creek trail, #1511, about three and a half flat miles to where it meets Leroy Creek near 4,120 to 4,140 ft. Cross on a large tree or by rock-hopping — awkward in early season with the creek up — and pick up the well-worn but unsigned climbers' trail, #1512, on the north side of the creek. It is sometimes called the Carne Mountain High Route, but the two are also treated as different paths, so do not assume the names are interchangeable. It climbs steeply, then eases into the Leroy Creek Basin meadow at about 6,100 ft, roughly five miles from the car and a little over two hours for a party moving well with light packs. Good camping and water. Above the basin, one party continued on the high-route path less than a quarter mile and then went directly into the upper basin below Maude by way of a gully with a small waterfall. Keep climbing cross-country over meadow, scrub, talus and probably snow to the Seven Fingered Jack / Maude col at about 8,150 ft, north-west of Maude's summit.

ways.name: Entiat River and Ice Lakes from the east — the first-ascent line
ways.season: Same window; this side is a much longer walk and is mostly used by parties already camped at Ice Lakes or exiting that way
ways.notes:
Drive the Entiat River Road and walk the Entiat River trail #1400 about eight and a quarter miles to the Ice Creek trail. The Entiat River has to be crossed on logs, and if there is no log at the trail there may be a large jam south of it.

The first-ascent party did not follow the river to the meadows at its head. They walked instead to the col between Spectacle Buttes and Maude's south-east side and dropped from Ice Lakes onto the slopes beside the face, judging it more direct and free of bushwhacking. That cost them nearly three thousand feet of climbing to reach Ice Lakes.

ways.name: Winter and spring: Commonwealth Basin from Summit West, straight at the gully
ways.season: Roughly December to April, once the gully has filled and consolidated — that is also exactly when the avalanche problem is live, so the NWAC Snoqualmie Pass forecast is a mandatory read
ways.notes:
The fast winter line does not start at Alpental. Park at Summit West and walk the short distance to the start of the winter Commonwealth ski and snowshoe trail, which is usually well compacted. Cross the log and head directly at the route.

Where the ground steepens, trend far left until you come up against huge cliffs, then go about 100 ft further left again and climb to the start of the gully. The whole approach is about a mile and takes roughly an hour on firm snow.

The adjacent Summit at Snoqualmie ski area does avalanche control on nearby slopes in season; check with the resort before a winter attempt.

ways.name: Summer and autumn: the south side of the peak from Alpental, as a dry scramble
ways.season: Roughly June to October as an easy-fifth-class rock scramble — a completely different and lower-consequence outing from the winter climb
ways.notes:
From I-90 exit 52, follow Alpental Road up to the ski area. Guye Peak's rock rises directly above the parking area, so there is essentially no approach walk to the south-side routes. Respect the posted no-parking signs on the private sections of road; access on foot through the Alpental Community Club's private ground has been closed to climbers, so plan a line from public ground.

Once below the peak, find the obvious gully on the south side and scramble it.

The summer version of this line is not well loved: discontinuous rock, vegetation, deep pine needles and general gully looseness are what a dry ascent actually delivers.

ways.name: Canyon Creek trailhead, Crater Lake, and the traverse over the Jerry Glacier
ways.season: Mid-July through September, for dry rock on the crest and a crossable Jerry Glacier
ways.notes: Identical to the South Face as far as camp. From the Canyon Creek Trailhead near 1,900 ft, ford Canyon Creek - there is no bridge, and it runs high and hazardous in spring and early summer, so look at it before you commit - and grind up Trail #738's switchbacks through forest to the Crater Lake trail junction. Carry water from the creek; the hillside above has none. Continue past Crater Lake and up long exposed switchbacks, then leave the tread between about 6,700 and 7,200 ft and traverse to the saddle between Crater Mountain's summit and its east peak near 7,200 ft. Descend steep snow and the crevassed Jerry Glacier, cross the saddle above Jerry Lakes, and camp at the lakes near 6,400 ft or in the Crater Creek meadows near 6,000 ft.

ways.name: Two camps at the end of the same approach: Jerry Lakes or Crater Creek Meadows
ways.season: Same window; the meadows hold running water later than the snow patches above the lakes
ways.notes: The fork is only about where you sleep. The lakes near 6,400 ft are the shorter day in with water at the tent. Crossing the notch just south of the lakes and dropping into Crater Creek Basin to camp in the meadows near 6,000 ft costs a descent and a re-ascent but starts summit day on the correct side of the notch, directly under the shoulder where the ridge is gained.

ways.name: East Face from the SR-20 hairpin pullout
ways.season: Jul-Sep (dry talus)
ways.notes:
This route is on the east side of the mountain and is not approached from the Blue Lake Trailhead. Drive to the hairpin turn on SR-20 a short way east of Washington Pass and park in the turnout there.

Walk back along the road toward the pass until you see the small pond on the south side of the highway. The boot path starts at the pond's east end and goes north into the timber; it is cairned, but the cairns are easy to lose in the dark on a pre-dawn start, so scout the first few minutes in daylight the evening before if you can.

The path climbs steeply through forest and then breaks out onto the talus directly under the East Face. Reported times run from about half an hour to an hour of steep walking. There is no water on this approach — carry it from the car.

One consequence worth planning for: if you continue to the true summit and take the standard notch descent, you come down on the west side of the mountain and will need a shuttle or a road walk back to the hairpin. Some parties instead rappel the East Face to return directly to their packs.

ways.name: Early-season snow and moat at the East Face base
ways.season: Late spring / early summer after the highway opens, while snow still covers the talus
ways.notes:
Same trailhead and same cairned path from the pond's east end, but early in the season the talus under the wall is buried in snow that firms up hard overnight. Parties have reported chipping steps in icy snow to reach the rock, and finding the snow lying steeply enough that a slip would carry you a long way down the slope.

Carry an axe and traction, and expect to be in boots for the walk in even when the wall itself is dry.

ways.name: Commonwealth Basin and Lundin Basin
ways.season: Jun-Jul on snow is the good window; brushy and slow once melted out
ways.notes:
From the PCT-North / Commonwealth Basin trailhead off the Alpental road (about 3,000 ft), follow the Pacific Crest Trail northbound; within roughly half a mile bear left onto the Commonwealth Basin use trail, which climbs gently along Commonwealth Creek through old-growth for about 1.7 miles as the valley opens out.

Near 4,200 ft leave the main Red Pass tread and cut west, contouring into Lundin Basin below Red Mountain's south face. From there climb a broad couloir — snow in early season, scree and talus by late summer — up the steep south side of Lundin to gain the West Ridge at its notch.

This is much the better line while snow still covers the basin: it buries the brush and the boulders, and parties report a long glissade on the way out. Once melted out the lower basin is brushy with steep scree and talus, and that is the reason many parties switch to the Cave Ridge approach late in the season.

Commonwealth Creek is reliable water low down; nothing above is dependable, so fill up in the basin.

ways.name: Cave Ridge traverse from Alpental
ways.season: Jul-Oct; the better late-season option
ways.notes:
Park at the Alpental day-use lot and find the unmarked, unmaintained Snoqualmie Mountain climbers' trail that starts about 50 ft south of the signed Snow Lake trailhead. It crosses below a small waterfall and climbs steeply through forest and slide alder.

At an unsigned split around 4,600 ft, paths fork toward Snoqualmie Mountain, Cave Ridge and Lundin. Take the Cave Ridge / Lundin fork, cross over Cave Ridge near its low notch, then follow an ascending climbers'-trail traverse below the ridge crest — staying on the Commonwealth Basin, north, side — to the West Ridge notch.

This skirts the brushy lower basin entirely, which is why parties prefer it once the snow has gone. There is no reliable water past the trailhead.

ways.name: Hannegan Pass, Chilliwack River and Whatcom Pass, then around Whatcom Peak to Perfect Pass
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. The Whatcom Glacier traverse is the season-limiting piece: in low-snow years it has been reported down to bare ice with open crevasses
ways.notes:
From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at the end of FS Road 32 (Ruth Creek Road) off WA-542, Trail #674 climbs a well-graded 2,000 ft over 4 miles to Hannegan Pass at about 5,100 ft. That pass is the last easy water and the point where the two approaches to Challenger split.

This one drops the far side, losing roughly 2,500 ft into the Chilliwack River valley at Boundary Camp, crosses the Chilliwack, and follows the Chilliwack River Trail past Copper Creek Camp to the Whatcom Pass backcountry camp. Log crossings of the Chilliwack are unreliable and have caught out parties who lost the crossing and had to bushwhack.

From Whatcom Pass you still have to get round Whatcom Peak. The direct North Ridge is loose, extremely exposed and not recommended for most parties; the standard workaround traverses the Whatcom Glacier on Whatcom Peak's east side. Treat that as glacier travel.

ways.name: Hannegan Pass, then Easy Ridge and the Impasse to Perfect Pass
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. Snow in the Impasse notch can make the direct crossing either easier or impossible depending on the year
ways.notes:
The alternative from the same trailhead. From the Chilliwack River Trail below Hannegan Pass, ford the Chilliwack again near Easy Ridge and climb steeply onto the ridge, site of an old fire lookout. A faint climbers' path follows the crest past tarns and slabby sections, over Easy Peak, to a notch known as the Impasse, then continues cross-country toward Perfect Pass.

Round trip via Easy Ridge alone runs about 26 miles; the full car-to-summit distance by either line is roughly 37 miles, so most parties treat this as a 3-5 day trip with camps at Whatcom Pass or Perfect Pass, or both.

ways.name: Merritt Lake Trailhead and Nason Ridge Trail to Crescent Lake
ways.season: July into October once the ridge clears; snow persists above about 5,000 ft into late spring.
ways.notes: The shorter and more direct way in. From the highway turn onto the rough forest road — high clearance is worth having — and drive to the Merritt Lake Trailhead. Climb the Merritt Lake trail to the lake, then join the Nason Ridge Trail and follow it east to Crescent Lake, which sits below the peak's south side. Water is available at Crescent Lake but is unreliable higher on the mountain, so fill there. The trail is well defined the whole way to the lake, and everything above it is your own route-finding.

ways.name: Rock Mountain Trailhead via Rock Lake and the Rock–Crescent col
ways.season: July into October. Snow lingers above about 5,000 ft into late spring and the col holds it longest.
ways.notes: The longer and more scenic way in, and the one commonly used by parties who want the neighbouring summit in the same outing. From the highway near the milepost, climb the Rock Mountain trail to Rock Lake — snow persists above about 5,000 ft into late spring on this side — then cross the col between the two peaks and descend roughly five hundred feet on the far side to Crescent Lake. From there the climb is the same as from the other trailhead. It costs a substantial descent that has to be regained on the return, which is the price of the extra ground it covers.

ways.name: Paradise, the Nisqually crossing and the Wilson bench
ways.season: Mid-May into early August; the approach and glaciers deteriorate quickly after that
ways.notes:
From Paradise (5,420 ft) follow the paved trail about a mile to Glacier Vista, then the Nisqually Moraine climbers' path to roughly 6,300 ft where boot paths drop onto the Nisqually Glacier. Rope up here — the crossing is through crevassed ground exposed to icefall from above and is dangerous in poor visibility.

From the east side of the glacier there are two ways onto the Wapowety Cleaver ground. One is a flat traverse to the base of a gully known as The Fan, climbed directly to a bench at about 7,300 ft; The Fan carries avalanche, rockfall and steep-snow hazard. The other climbs the Nisqually/Wilson margin at about 6,800 ft through an often-crevassed gully to the same 7,300–7,400 ft bench.

Above the bench, snow slopes lead to a string of established camps: Wilson Moraine (8,200–8,600 ft), Lower Castle (9,250 ft) and Upper Castle (9,400–9,500 ft), the most common base, with running water from about mid-June. Higher again, rock islands along the west edge of the Turtle snowfield between roughly 9,500 and 10,500 ft hold good bivouacs, and there is usually flowing water at the snowfield edges in warm weather.

Camp Hazard (about 10,800 ft) is the traditional high camp and is named for what sits above it: the Kautz Ice Cliff. Many parties deliberately camp lower and climb through Camp Hazard early rather than sleep under the cliff. On the Turtle, keep to the western, climber's-left side — the centre and east are raked by ice and rock off the cliff.

Rainier permits apply: a per-person climbing permit for glacier travel or ground above roughly 10,000 ft, and a wilderness permit for each overnight camp in the high-use season.

ways.name: Comet Falls and Van Trump Park
ways.season: Same window; avoids the Nisqually Glacier crossing entirely
ways.notes:
Start at the Comet Falls trailhead (3,650 ft) on the Longmire–Paradise road. The maintained Comet Falls Trail climbs 2.2 miles and about 2,000 ft to a junction, then continues toward Van Trump Park for another 0.6 miles to the end of maintained tread. From there unmaintained social trails climb a steep moraine crest to about 6,500 ft and onto the permanent snow of the Van Trump Glacier remnant, which is followed to the Upper Castle at roughly 9,500 ft where this approach merges with the Paradise line.

The advantage is that it never crosses the Nisqually Glacier. The cost is a lower start, a steeper carry and a descent that is genuinely hard to reverse: the Park Service's own advice is to save a GPS track, because relocating the correct moraine and the treeline trail junction on the way down is difficult even in clear weather. Several parties a season lose that junction and end up bushwhacking.

ways.name: White Salmon Lodge road
ways.season: spring; snow cover strongly preferred
ways.notes: Small pull-off at the old White Salmon lodge on the Mount Baker Highway. Walk around the gate and take the old road past the lodge site for about a mile until it ends at an old clearcut. With good snow, descend northeast to White Salmon Creek and follow the valley up to the toe of the glacier. Without good snow, do NOT go down into the valley — hold your height entering the clearcut and contour, shedding elevation only to get around rock bands and stream crossings. This is the same decision that governs the North Face approach, and it is the difference between a walk and a fight with slide alder. Going south past Lake Ann and over Austin Pass is not the way parties reach the White Salmon Glacier; the drainage is entered from the White Salmon side of the highway.

ways.name: Mount Baker Ski Area (Chair 8) traverse
ways.season: winter/spring, on skis
ways.notes: From the base of Chair 8, traverse downhill into the bottom of the White Salmon Creek valley and then climb over four thousand feet to near the base of Hell's Highway at the top of the glacier. This is the ski-descent party's usual line in.

ways.name: Duckabush River Trail to the unmarked creek turnoff
ways.season: Mid-July to September
ways.notes: Twenty-odd miles up the Duckabush over Big Hump, with a wide ford of the river above Duckabush Camp that runs thigh-deep and swift in early season. The climbers' line leaves the maintained trail roughly three miles below Marmot Lake. A multi-day backpack with a high camp at the lake or in the basin, never a car-to-car day.

ways.name: First Divide and the unnamed lake basin
ways.season: Mid-July to September
ways.notes: Parties generally find this the easier of the two lines and it is much shorter, but the corridor on that side has been closed by fire damage — confirm before planning around it. From the divide the route runs west into a basin, then over a col and north along the crest.

ways.name: Blue Lake Trail to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch
ways.season: Jul-Sep
ways.notes:
Identical to the Beckey Route walk-in, which is why the two are so often climbed on the same day. Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft) on SR-20 about 1 mile west of Washington Pass; about 1.75 miles of maintained trail to the signed Liberty Bell Trail #727 climbing-access junction just past a small stream, marked with a large cairn; then the climbers' path up slabs, talus and heather into the bowl below the towers and up the gully to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch at about 7,300 ft.

In the gully, staying climber's left for the lower two thirds and then crossing to climber's right keeps you on the most stable ground.

ways.name: Early-season snow to the notch
ways.season: Highway opening through late Jun
ways.notes:
Same line, but the gully feeding the Liberty Bell-Concord notch holds snow into late June most years and the boot path lower down may still be buried. Ice axe standard, crampons if it has refrozen.

One upside of the early season here: while the gully is snow-filled the rock in it is locked in place, and rockfall gets noticeably worse once it melts out.

SR-20 is closed across Washington Pass every winter, typically from late November or early December until mid-April to early May, so this window begins whenever the highway reopens.

ways.name: North side — Stuart Lake TH via Mountaineer Creek
ways.season: Jun to mid-Jul is the sweet spot; workable through Sep
ways.notes:
Park at the Stuart Lake Trailhead at the end of FR 7601 (Eightmile Road) out of Leavenworth and walk the Stuart Lake Trail up Mountaineer Creek. At the signed split roughly two miles along, ignore the Colchuck Lake branch on the right and carry straight on. A short distance further you leave maintained tread altogether, well before Stuart Lake, ford Mountaineer Creek and follow its south fork upstream cross-country. Late in the season there is a cairned climbers' path through much of this; early in the season there is not, and the creek runs hard.

Above the streamside travel a steep, unstable talus and boulder slope lifts you into the hanging basin under Sherpa Peak and the Sherpa Glacier. This basin holds the usual bivies. From it you angle up onto the glacier bench beneath the ridge.

This is the shorter, lower-gain way in and it puts you at the toe with the most in the tank, but it commits you to a car shuttle: the standard descent is the Cascadian Couloir, which spills out on the far side of the range at Ingalls Creek. Parties report the shuttle drive between the two trailheads costing several hours round trip. In June and early July the Sherpa Glacier is a reasonable way back down to this side and removes the shuttle problem — later in the summer it is not.

There is running snowmelt near the toe of the ridge (reported around 47.48095, -120.89454); above the 8,200 ft notch there is no reliable water once the last snow patch there melts out.

ways.name: South side — Esmeralda TH over Longs Pass and Goat Pass
ways.season: Jul-Sep, once the traverse under the Stuart Glacier has melted or consolidated
ways.notes:
From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway River Road (FR 9737), take the trail over Longs Pass and up Ingalls Creek to Goat Pass, then traverse east beneath the Stuart Glacier, staying above the large moraine mound, and aim for the toe of the ridge.

About 2,000 ft of the day is descent, so the round trip is more work than the raw gain suggests, and parties consistently report it taking longer than planned — budget eight hours and expect route-finding on the traverse rather than tread.

The reason to accept the longer, higher approach is that it removes the shuttle entirely. The Cascadian Couloir descent drops to Ingalls Creek on this side, so a party that walked in from Esmeralda walks out to its own car. Parties who came in from the north do not.

How much snow remains on the Goat Pass traverse is the recurring gear question here: sections have been reported at around 40 degrees, and whether you need an axe and traction changes week to week through the summer. Recent photos and current reports are worth more than any fixed answer.

ways.name: From the west: Hannegan Pass, the Chilliwack River Trail and Brush Creek to Whatcom Pass
ways.season: Jul-Sep
ways.notes:
About 16-17 miles one-way. Start at the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at the end of Hannegan Pass Road, FS-32, at about 3,100 ft, and follow Trail #674 about 4 miles and 2,000 ft to Hannegan Pass, then descend the far side to Boundary Camp in the Chilliwack River valley.

Continue down-valley on the Chilliwack River Trail, unmaintained and rough in sections with stretches obliterated by avalanche debris, past Copper Creek Camp and US Cabin Camp, cross the Chilliwack by the hand-operated cable car just beyond US Cabin (or ford it), then turn up the Brush Creek Trail at its junction near mile 12 and climb past Graybeal Camp and Whatcom Camp to Whatcom Pass. Typically split over two days with a valley-bottom camp.

ways.name: From the east: Ross Lake water taxi to Little Beaver, then 16 miles up-valley to Whatcom Pass
ways.season: Jul-Sep
ways.notes: Comparable in mileage to the western line. Hire a water taxi from Ross Lake Resort, near Diablo off SR-20, to the Little Beaver Creek trailhead at about 1,600 ft on Ross Lake, then follow the Little Beaver Trail roughly 16 miles up-valley, passing Perry Creek Camp at 4.6 miles and Twin Rocks Camp around mile 8, then the Big Beaver Trail junction at 10.5 miles, before the final steep switchback climb through big-fir forest up to Whatcom Pass.

ways.name: Gold Creek and the Crater Creek spur to the lake, then the south-east ridge
ways.season: Late July through September, once the upper ridge is out of snow
ways.notes:
From Twisp, run south on the highway to the Gold Creek loop and continue onto the Gold Creek road, which becomes forest road 4340 after several miles. Turn onto the Crater Creek spur and follow it a little under five miles to the trailhead at about 4,750 ft; a day-use fee or an interagency pass is required. The maintained trail climbs about four miles and roughly two thousand one hundred feet to Lower Crater Lake; the upper lake lies off to the south-south-west and is not on the way. From the lake the route leaves the trail and follows the south-east ridge to a col near 8,000 ft and on to the summit.

Be careful with names when planning this one: the lake and creek names in this part of the range repeat across neighbouring drainages, and there is an unrelated lake and mountain of the same name in a different part of the state entirely. Navigate by the road numbers you turned onto and the trailhead elevation you actually parked at.

ways.name: From the Libby Creek road and Trail #415, gaining the crest by the gully above the lake
ways.season: Late July through September, when the gully is free of snow
ways.notes:
The other drainage reaches the same crest. From the Libby Creek road system - a turn onto the main forest road, a left, a right onto a spur and a left onto a second spur - park at the small roadside trailhead between about 4,400 and 4,430 ft, with no toilet and no water. Trail #415 leads to the lake, past a dilapidated cabin used by some parties as a camp, with root holes and burn damage underfoot in the lower and middle miles.

This approach is shorter to the crest and pays for it with a single very loose gully, which is the crux of that side of the mountain.

ways.name: Burgundy Col and the glacier, in a day
ways.season: Jun-Sep
ways.notes:
Park at the pullout on SR-20 near milepost 166, about four miles east of Washington Pass. Drop the embankment — around 150 to 200 feet down loose ground — to Early Winters Creek and cross on a log; the logjam moves year to year, so scout, and be ready to ford in early-season high water.

On the far side pick up the well-defined climbers' path up the timbered rib on the west side of the Burgundy Creek drainage. It climbs steeply and almost without switchbacks. Treat the creek as your last reliable water.

Around 6,000 to 6,400 ft the grade eases at the bench, an open larch and heather shelf with established campsites. Above it, continue toward Burgundy Col — roughly 3,500 ft of gain from the highway to the col.

Do not take the obvious direct gully to the col: it is loose and exposed. Stay left, follow the trail up the gully directly above the camp area, and near its head make an ascending traverse right under the cliffs on heather-covered slabs into the col at about 7,770 ft.

ways.name: Camp at the bench, summit the second day
ways.season: Jun-Sep
ways.notes:
The same line from the milepost 166 pullout, broken at the open bench at roughly 6,000 to 6,400 ft where the climbers' path first eases. There are several established sites there, usually with a seasonal trickle or snowmelt nearby, and it is the standard overnight for this peak.

Camping here means you cross the glacier on firm morning snow and are back over the col before the afternoon softening, which matters given the reclimb to the col on the way out.

ways.name: The closed Kindy Creek roadbed and the Kindy Ridge climbers' path to the lake meadows
ways.season: June through September
ways.notes:
From Marblemount, drive the river road about fourteen miles and turn right onto forest road 1570, which crosses the river on a concrete bridge. Within roughly half a mile the right fork is blocked by boulders and washout; park at that Y-junction around 1,200 ft. The spur beyond is permanently closed to vehicles by windfall, brush and washouts, so the trip opens with a two to three mile road walk rather than at a trailhead.

The climbers' path above is unsigned and has no trail number, and it climbs hard through brush and then old growth on boot-beaten tread over roots and rock, with no water until well upslope. The grade eases at a boggy bench near 4,800 ft with room for a tent and seasonal water. Higher, a cairn-marked fork sends a fainter fisherman's trail down toward a lake; stay on the climbers' path. The ridge then rolls constantly over several small points rather than climbing steadily, before dropping to the meadows by the lake, which are the best camp on the route.

ways.name: Two camps: the lake meadows or the benches above them
ways.season: Same window; the higher benches are wind-exposed with limited flat ground
ways.notes: The meadows by the lake are the most established camp on the route, with reliable water and good tent sites. The rock and snow benches above, around 6,200 ft, shorten summit day but are exposed and take the wind, with limited flat ground for tents. Parties splitting the approach over two days also use the boggy bench near 4,800 ft as a low camp, where the water is seasonal and can be down to puddles late in the year.

ways.name: Hannegan Pass, the Chilliwack ford and Easy Ridge over the Imperfect Impasse to Perfect Pass
ways.season: Jul-Sep
ways.notes:
From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at the end of Hannegan Pass Road, FS-32, off SR-542 at about 3,100 ft, Trail #674 runs about 4 miles and 2,000 ft to Hannegan Pass at roughly 5,050-5,100 ft. The trail then switchbacks down the far side into the Chilliwack River valley to Boundary Camp and continues down-valley to the Chilliwack River crossing.

That ford is the approach's main hazard: it can be thigh-deep and swift at mid-summer flow, and is harder earlier in the season or after rain. From the ford, leave the maintained trail system and pick up the old, unmaintained Easy Ridge climbers' trail, which climbs steeply out of the valley to Easy Saddle at about 5,200 ft, a common camp, roughly 5.5 to 8.5 hours and 8-9 miles in depending on pace and the ford.

From Easy Saddle the route follows the crest over or around Easy Peak at 6,613 ft to the Imperfect Impasse, then continues to Perfect Pass at about 6,200 ft, the standard high camp, about 16 miles in, commonly the end of a second day, though fast parties reach it in one. There is no reliable water at Perfect Pass in late season; fill at Easy Saddle or from snowmelt.

ways.name: The low-orbit traverse from Whatcom Pass, skipping Easy Ridge and the Impasse entirely
ways.season: Jul-Sep; treat as glacier travel in early season
ways.notes:
An alternative that avoids the Impasse. From Whatcom Pass, reached via the Chilliwack River and Brush Creek trails or via the Little Beaver Creek Trail from Ross Lake, a low-orbit traverse around Whatcom Peak's east side on scree and snow reaches the same south-side snowfields.

From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at about 3,100 ft at the end of Ruth Creek Road, FR-32, off the Mt. Baker Highway, Trail #674 runs 4.2-4.6 miles and about 2,000 ft alongside Ruth Creek to Hannegan Pass at 5,066 ft, the last easy reliable water before dropping into the national park.

From the pass, descend the Chilliwack River Trail through long viewless switchbacks, losing roughly 2,800 ft, past Boundary and Copper Creek camps. The river is crossed via a hand-pulled cable car near US Cabin Camp rather than a ford, which is the practical difference between this and the Easy Ridge approach.

Continue up-valley on the Brush Creek Trail toward Graybeal Camp, roughly 14 trail miles and a cumulative 4,400 ft of gain from the trailhead. The small creek near Graybeal is unreliable and can run dry by late summer, so fill earlier at the Chilliwack or US Cabin Camp. Past Graybeal the maintained tread gives way to a steep, brushy, root-and-timber climbers' path gaining roughly 2,000 ft over the final 3 miles to Whatcom Pass at 5,206 ft, passing Whatcom Camp and the first real views of the Challenger Glacier.

ways.name: Lena Lake and the Brothers climbers' path (summer)
ways.season: Jun-Sep; by late August the couloir is often scrambling rather than snow
ways.notes:
Lena Lake Trailhead (Trail #810) off FS-25, around 700 ft. About 3 miles and 1,100 ft of gain on maintained trail through second- and old-growth, crossing several creek drainages, to Lena Lake at roughly 1,800 ft — a busy backpacking destination with a ranger station, and the last easy reliable water and camping before the climbers' route.

Skirt the west side of the lake and pick up the unmaintained but well-trodden Brothers boot path, which follows the East Fork Lena Creek drainage through the old-growth known as the Valley of the Silent Men for roughly 2.5-3 miles to a climbers' camp around 2,900 ft, marked by a fire ring. Most parties use this as high camp for a two-day ascent.

Route-finding gets hardest immediately after leaving camp for the summit push, where the boot path repeatedly appears to vanish. Follow a climbers' path upstream and west along the west fork for about a mile. It crosses an avalanche debris field where slide alder and downed logs — some with hand-lines or steps cut into them — hide the line, and creek fords may be needed. Beyond the debris field the path re-enters forest and climbs toward the couloir.

Water is reliable at the lake and up Lena Creek to high camp. Above camp there is nothing dependable once you are on scree and snow.

ways.name: Early-season snow ascent
ways.season: Apr-May, snow
ways.notes:
The classic time for this route is early season, roughly April into May, because the gullies fill in with dense brush later and the snow-covered version is much faster.

The approach is the same — Lena Lake, the Brothers boot path up the East Fork, the climbers' camp near 2,900 ft — but the avalanche debris field between camp and the couloir is easier under snow, and the couloir itself becomes a snow climb requiring an axe and reliable self-arrest rather than a scree slog.

Snow also buries the boot path, so the route-finding difficulty immediately above camp is worse, not better: there is no tread to find at all.

ways.name: Over the pass at the head of the river road, then east and down to the lake
ways.season: Spring into early summer, while the couloir still holds continuous snow
ways.notes:
From the trailhead at the end of the river road, climb to the pass at about 5,392 ft - or to the nearby col used as an alternative when the pass is corniced - and then travel east, descending and traversing through the basin beyond, to the lake at about 4,170 ft, which sits just north-east of the peak. From the lake you boot or skin directly to the foot of the route, changing to crampons or ascent plates as the snow firms up higher.

This is the approach that suits the route's season: the couloir is a snow line, so the party wants it early, which is also when the pass is a straightforward snow climb rather than a scramble.

ways.name: From the valley on the east, reaching the lake basin from below
ways.season: Summer, once the valley trail is open and the basin is snow-free enough to walk
ways.notes:
The lake basin can also be reached from the valley to the east, which is entered by boat or floatplane and then by road and trail up the valley floor. This is the approach the other route on this peak uses, and it puts a party at the lake without any pass to cross.

Treat the detail of it with caution. The published descriptions of this peak disagree about which drainage is followed off the valley trail and how far the lake is from the road, and the two accounts cannot both be right - so plan this variant from current maps and imagery rather than from a written description, and expect the off-trail section to be unmarked and steep.

ways.name: Niederprum Trail #653 to Lone Tree Pass and High Pass
ways.season: late Apr-Jun for snow cover; the line goes later but on more rock
ways.notes:
Niederprum trailhead at the end of Old Mine Road above Darrington. The Moose Creek bridge just past the gate has been closed and barricaded for years, so parties park at the gate, get past the barricade on foot and walk the road roughly a mile and a quarter to the real trailhead — extra distance and gain that older published figures do not include.

Trail #653 switchbacks through forest into the Boulder River Wilderness and reaches 'the flat' at about 3,200 ft, a level clearing on the site of an old mining cabin and the natural rest or camp spot. Beyond it the maintained tread ends and a boot path threads thinning, brushy forest with deadfall.
