From the Hannegan Trailhead at 3,100 ft at the end of Ruth Creek Road, the Hannegan Pass Trail runs about 4 miles and 2,500 ft to Hannegan Pass at 5,066 ft, then drops off the north side into the Chilliwack River valley and loses most of the gain again.

The valley traverse passes Copper Creek Camp around mile 9 and U.S. Cabin Camp around mile 12; expect brushy tread near U.S. Cabin and, in blowdown years, real timber. One party logged roughly two hours to move 1.5 miles through fallen trunks beyond the cable-car crossing. The Chilliwack is crossed on a hand-pulled cable car, which is mandatory and somewhat exposed; the river is not reliably fordable.

Beyond it the Brush Creek Trail climbs to Whatcom Pass at 5,206 ft, roughly 17 miles in. From Whatcom Camp, leave trail and traverse below Whatcom Peak's northeast flank on the Whatcom Glacier to Perfect Pass, about 4.5 hours and 1,750 ft. Perfect Pass has reliable running water and is a common high camp. From there rope up, climb the Challenger Glacier to a high bench near 8,100 ft, and descend through West Challenger Notch onto the Crooked Thumb Glacier. Round trip is on the order of 40 miles.

ways.name: Big Beaver valley and Wiley Ridge
ways.notes: Take the water taxi from Ross Lake Resort to the Big Beaver landing and follow the Big Beaver trail up the valley toward Luna Camp. Leave the trail and climb Wiley Ridge off-trail to the basin on its south side, then continue to the Challenger Arm and cross to West Challenger Notch above the Crooked Thumb Glacier. Expect several days and serious bushwhacking.

ways.name: The SR-20 South Buttress pullout, then bear right into the basin beneath the North Ridge Notch
ways.season: Jul-Sep
ways.notes:
The standard approach uses the same SR-20 pullout as the South Buttress, on the north side of the highway about 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass. Follow the South Buttress approach: creek crossing, brushy climbers' path into the meadow, up into the boulder field.

Eight pitches at 5.7. It sees far less traffic than the South Buttress, the peak's classic line.

ways.name: Rainy Pass and Porcupine Creek into the basin northwest of the peak
ways.notes: From Rainy Pass, follow the PCT north for about twenty minutes and leave it before the Porcupine Creek bridge, climbing through timber into the basin northwest of the peak. Two or three short low-fifth pitches reach the North Ridge notch. Longer than the south-side basin, but on cleaner rock to the notch; parties camped near Rainy Pass or combining objectives use it.

ways.name: Bean Creek Trail to Earl Pass
ways.season: Class 2 on dry ground from July into October, and a popular spring snow climb before that, when an axe and sometimes crampons are wanted on the steep south-facing summit slopes.
ways.notes: From the road-end trailhead start north on the Beverly Turnpike Trail #1391, a mellow stretch of old roadbed beside Beverly Creek, and at the signed junction bear right and east onto the Bean Creek Trail; the Turnpike Trail carries straight on up the wrong valley for this peak. The Bean Creek tread climbs through forest into a tight, steep-sided valley, drops to a ford of Bean Creek, then keeps climbing until the forest breaks open into a broad flower meadow with old-growth stands and several informal camping flats. That basin is the last dependable water. At the meadow fork bear right and east rather than left into the upper basin; tread goes intermittent through the upper meadows before switchbacking to a broad saddle on the divide.

ways.name: Standup Creek trail
ways.notes: From the Standup Creek trailhead, the trail runs up a gentle valley, then steepens through open hillside to the southwest ridge of Earl Peak, where a boot path leads to the summit. Quieter and gentler at first than the Bean Creek side, with the hard climbing saved for the upper slopes.

ways.name: North Fork Entiat Trail #1437 to the meadow camp
ways.season: Mid-July into early October. Snow can hold in the gullies well into the season, and an axe is worth carrying early and mid-season.
ways.notes: Drive the Entiat River Road and then the switchbacking forest-road spur to the North Fork Entiat Trailhead, and follow North Fork Entiat River Trail #1437 up-valley. Almost all of the distance to the peak is on trail. The usual staging point is the trail camp in the meadow below the summit around 6,700 ft, and the climb starts from the tread a short way north of it. A boat-access alternative exists on the far side, reaching the peak from Emerald Park via Trail #1230 out of the lakeshore settlement; it is a genuine second way in, but where that line joins the climbing is unclear, so the base-finding below is written for the trail camp side.

ways.name: Emerald Park trail from Lucerne
ways.notes: Take the boat up Lake Chelan to Lucerne, follow the Domke Lake trail to the Emerald Park trail, and climb up Emerald Park to Milham Pass, which drops into the basin between Emerald and Saska. A boat-dependent alternative to the Entiat side, and the natural choice when coming from Lake Chelan.

ways.name: Basalt Ridge crest to Fifth of July Pass
ways.season: Mid-July through early October, and popular in early autumn for the larch.
ways.notes: This is the shorter alternative to the Entiat River approach. From the Basalt Pass trailhead, climb to the pass — the small stream in the gully below it is the last water, and there is none at all beyond — then follow the ridge north. The trail bypasses the first high point about 300 ft below it, and beyond the trail fork the tread fades into slick pumice. Continue north past the neighbouring tower's saddle, then through a col around 7,480 ft on the next peak's southwest ridge, dropping through a scree gully into the basin west of it. Hop the massive boulders in that basin, cross a small larch meadow, and regain the ridge. The peak can also be reached from the Entiat River side by way of Myrtle Lake, the Larch Lakes and Cow Creek Pass — that is the line the main approach and waypoints describe; the marks below are written for this Basalt Ridge side.

ways.name: Entiat River and Larch Lakes
ways.notes: From the trailhead at the end of the Entiat River road, follow the Entiat River trail up the valley and climb the side trail to the Larch Lakes meadows. From a camp between the lakes the summit is a modest day out along the ridge. Longer than the Basalt Ridge line, but on maintained trail with water, so it suits multi-day trips and loops.

ways.name: Devore Creek Trail from Bird Creek Camp over the Enigma saddle
ways.season: Midsummer into early autumn, and tied to the boat and shuttle timetable at both ends.
ways.notes: Come up the lake by passenger ferry or floatplane, ride the shuttle up the valley road to the bridge, cross it and follow the road past the camp and the airstrip to pick up the river trail. Follow that mostly flat trail southeast to the signed Devore Creek Trail junction, then climb steeply through rock bluffs and open forest into the wilderness and traverse brushy, dry hillside to Bird Creek Camp — the only designated camp in that stretch of trail, sitting about fifty yards before the creek crossing, with room for about three tents and a cook area. From camp the peak is a long day of its own; it does not combine with the neighbouring summit above the same camp, and every account allows a full day for each.

ways.name: Holden Village over Tenmile Pass
ways.notes: From Holden, climb to Tenmile Pass, descend the shoulder into upper Riddle Creek, then traverse northeast into the Castle Creek basin to join the standard line around 6,500 ft. Longer and more involved than Devore Creek; mostly used to combine Flora with Riddle Peak, or by parties exiting to Holden after climbing from Stehekin.

ways.name: White Chuck River and Kennedy Ridge to the Glacier Creek camps
ways.season: Roughly Jun-Aug, and it is one of the shorter windows on the mountain — the upper Kennedy is a small, steep glacier that opens into a maze of 5-15 ft crevasses as the season runs on
ways.notes:
The historic line starts at the White Chuck River Trailhead at the end of FR-23 and follows Trail #643 about four miles, then Kennedy Ridge Trail #639 for 1.7 miles to the Pacific Crest Trail near 5,000 ft. Turn north on the PCT and follow it about two miles to the Glacier Creek crossing, where there are established camps with reliable water near 5,300 ft. Four to five hours is the usual pack-in.

FR-23 has been closed from milepost 3.7 to its end, so the reliably open option in recent seasons has been the North Fork Sauk Trail and the PCT over Red Pass to the same Glacier Creek camps. That is a much longer walk to the same place, and it changes nothing above camp.

From the Glacier Creek camp a climbers' trail runs up a gully to the crest of Kennedy Ridge. Everything above is glacier, and the character of the day is set by how well you read the upper glacier rather than by any technical difficulty — the headwall at the top is about 40 degrees and short, while the crevasse field below it is the part parties spend hours on.

ways.name: North Fork Sauk and the crest trail north
ways.notes: Walk the North Fork Sauk trail up the valley and climb to the crest trail near White Pass, then follow it north past Red Pass, across the White Chuck basin and on toward Kennedy Creek, descending to the bench below the glacier. Long, with real elevation loss on the way, but this is how most parties now reach the Kennedy side.

ways.name: Ross Lake to May Creek and the Nohokomeen Glacier
ways.season: Mid-July to mid-September
ways.notes: A genuinely remote three-day outing on a mountain that sees almost no traffic, and the approach is the hard part of it. Parties reach May Creek Camp on the east shore of Ross Lake at about 1,600 ft either by walking seven or eight flat miles of the East Bank Trail from SR 20 or, far more often, by taking the resort water taxi, which removes nearly all of that. From the lake it is a few thousand feet of steep forest, and the trick is finding the open timber rather than fighting brush: parties who get it right leave the trail in open forest a couple of hundred yards from the junction, angle left of the fall line, and follow game trails through the rock bands between roughly 3,500 and 4,100 ft, where a short cliff step sometimes carries webbing left behind by earlier parties. Reaching the ridge crest around 5,000 ft, traverse to the top of the moraine, pass under the toe of the Nohokomeen Glacier and climb slabs on its left side to camp at about 6,700 ft. Some parties push on and camp higher on the glacier near 7,400 ft. The glacier above is usually straightforward and largely crack-free to its top at about 8,000 ft. Most parties climb this ridge and descend the East Ridge, which turns the trip into a traverse and puts the exit out to Jerry Lakes and the Crater Mountain trail rather than back down the timber.

ways.name: East Bank Trail on foot to May Creek
ways.notes: Walk the East Bank Trail from SR-20 north along the east shore of Ross Lake to May Creek Camp, where climbers leave the trail. Several hours of flat walking each way, but it needs no booking and works whenever the highway is open.

ways.name: North Fork Sauk Trail #649 to White Pass, then the Foam Basin traverse and the White Chuck Glacier
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. Late summer opens the crevasses so you can see and weave them; early season covers them with bridges you cannot read, and puts Red Creek and Lightning Creek in flood
ways.notes: From the North Fork Sauk Trailhead near 2,050 ft at the end of FR-49, Trail #649 runs about 5.5 miles up the valley on an easy grade through old growth, fording several tributaries. Red Creek is the first crossing that can actually stop you: manageable at normal flow, considerably higher during snowmelt or after rain, and worth a pole. Mackinaw Shelter at 2,950 ft is a possible camp but tight for a big party, and it is where the trail leaves the river — fill water there. Above the shelter the trail climbs about 3.2 miles of sustained switchbacks to a meadow junction with the Pacific Crest Trail near 6,000 ft, then a quarter mile north on the PCT to White Pass at 5,900 ft. That is roughly nine miles and 4,800 ft from the car and the last easy water before the high traverse. Maintained trail ends at the pass. Traverse north below the White Mountain ridge into Foam Basin and White River Meadows around 6,300-6,500 ft — the usual base camp — either by way of Red Pass or by crossing snowfields to the notch west of Point 6770 and dropping into the White Chuck basin. Almost nobody does this from the car in a day, and the round trip is long enough that the two published distances for it disagree.

ways.name: White River trail from the east
ways.notes: From the White River trailhead beyond Lake Wenatchee, walk the White River trail about 10 miles up the valley to the Lightning Creek crossing, then go cross-country up into the high basin east of the peaks. About as far on foot as the Sauk side, with less trail and more off-trail travel.

ways.name: Lake of the Woods camp and the east ridge
ways.season: July to early October
ways.notes: There is no trail on the mountain itself; the whole climb is talus, scree and boulder-field walking off a high camp. The usual staging is a camp around 6,600 ft near Lake of the Woods, reached over Pistol Pass on the long-abandoned Pistol Ridge tread out of the Monument Creek valley. That approach has been unmaintained for decades and involves an unbridged ford of Eureka Creek that runs thigh to waist deep during snowmelt. A longer alternative from the Slate Pass road end reaches the same country by way of the Ferguson Lake trail and avoids that ford, at the cost of tread that is harder still to follow. From camp the peak is a couple of hours each way for a fit party, and most parties pair it with Monument Peak.

ways.name: Slate Pass and the Pasayten side
ways.notes: Start high at Slate Pass on the Harts Pass road and drop toward the Middle Fork Pasayten, then work east by Eureka Creek and around into the basin below the peak. Longer and more cross-country than Pistol Pass, but it starts thousands of feet higher.

name: West Face - West Rib (Lichtenhorn / West Peak)

ways.name: Smith Brook road trailhead via Union Gap
ways.notes: From the trailhead on Smith Brook road, climb to Union Gap on the crest trail and follow it toward Lake Valhalla and Lichtenberg Pass, then leave the trail for the base of the west face.

ways.name: Crest trail north from Stevens Pass
ways.notes: Park in the north lot at Stevens Pass and follow the crest trail north to Lake Valhalla, arriving from the west below the face. It is a few miles longer than the Smith Brook start but needs no gravel road, and it is the usual start when Smith Brook road is under snow.

ways.name: Fryingpan Creek, Summerland and Meany Crest to Whitman Notch
ways.season: Roughly Jun through Aug, best early July to early August — firm morning snow, drier rock, and bridges not yet melted out
ways.notes:
Start at the Fryingpan Creek Trailhead near 3,800-3,900 ft on the Sunrise and White River Road, a few miles past the White River entrance station. Follow the signed trail up through old-growth beside Fryingpan Creek.

At roughly 3.2 miles and about 1,400 ft of gain there is an established footlog crossing of Fryingpan Creek — the main water and a spot that needs care in high runoff. Continue to Summerland at about 4.5 miles and roughly 5,900 ft: patrol cabin, pit toilet, bear wires, and the last reliable running water.

From Summerland leave maintained trail and take the climbers' path northwest of the campground knoll, up steep tundra and snow on the Meany Snowfield to Meany Crest, a rock outcrop at roughly 7,350-7,500 ft with flat sites and stone wind breaks. This is the standard high camp.

Above Meany Crest gain the toe of the Fryingpan Glacier and rope up. Climb south and southwest across the lower apron to the broad notch between the Fryingpan and Whitman glaciers at about 9,000-9,100 ft, then traverse and climb the upper Whitman across a bergschrund to about 10,500-11,000 ft, where snow gives way to rock.

The basin holds heavy snow and the approach slopes can be avalanche terrain in soft early-season conditions. Afternoon whiteout and thunderstorm activity is common on Rainier's flanks.

ways.name: White River Campground and the Wonderland Trail to Summerland
ways.notes: The Fryingpan Creek trailhead and its spur trail are closed for the bridge replacement, planned to last into 2029. Park at White River Campground, where parking is limited, and follow the Wonderland Trail to Summerland. From Summerland the climb is unchanged: the climbers' path to Meany Crest, the Fryingpan Glacier and Whitman Notch.

ways.name: From Paradise across the Cowlitz and Ingraham glaciers
ways.season: Nov-May, while the White River road to Summerland is shut
ways.notes:
From the Paradise parking lot, climb the standard Camp Muir route to about 8,600 ft. Leave it there and traverse east onto the Paradise Glacier and across the Cowlitz, holding elevation to stay above the cliff and serac band below, then through a notch in the Cathedral Rocks cleaver and across the Ingraham Glacier to a snow or rock ramp at the base of Little Tahoma's south and east face near 8,900 ft.

Camps are made on the Cowlitz or Ingraham glaciers, or on the more exposed Cathedral Rocks cleaver.

Above the ramp the route climbs the Whitman Glacier and exits its upper left-hand corner into a gully, climbs about two-thirds of it to a short step, continues up a gully-chimney to the summit notch, and finishes with a short loose scramble along the crest.

The Paradise road stays open far later into winter than the roads on the north and east sides, which is the whole reason this variant exists.

ways.name: Downey Creek, Bachelor Creek and Itswoot Ridge
ways.notes: From the Suiattle River Road, follow the Downey Creek trail up the valley, then turn up Bachelor Creek on a faint, brushy path toward Cub Lake and Itswoot Ridge. From the ridge, cross the glaciers east toward the Gunsight Range. Plan on a long two-day approach.

ways.name: From Stehekin up Agnes and Spruce Creeks
ways.notes: From High Bridge on the Stehekin Valley Road, follow the Pacific Crest Trail south up Agnes Creek about ten miles to the Spruce Creek confluence, crossing both creeks on logs. Then go cross-country, through dense brush, up toward the Icy-Spruce col for a high camp facing the Gunsights. Reaching Stehekin takes a boat or floatplane, so this is a multi-day trip.

ways.name: Lower Monument Basin and the left-angling ramp
ways.season: Mid-July to September
ways.notes: Monument is the most rugged thing in this group and sits nearly as an island, with Eureka Creek wrapping three sides of it. The travelled approach is the Monument Creek trail from the Lost River road: well maintained through old growth for about four miles to the Eureka Creek confluence, then unmaintained, brushy and deadfall-choked, with a ford of Eureka Creek that can run thigh to waist deep in early summer. From there the abandoned tread climbs onto Pistol Ridge and over Pistol Pass, and most parties camp near Lake of the Woods. Three other approaches exist off Slate Pass and Buckskin Ridge by way of the Ferguson Lake trail and reach the same basin from the north. Summit day is long enough that finishing the last talus by headlamp is common.

ways.name: From Slate Pass by Robinson Creek and the Ferguson Lake trail
ways.notes: Gentler, though not shorter. Drop north from Slate Pass to the Robinson Creek trail along the Middle Fork Pasayten, then near the big meadow horse camp take the Ferguson Lake trail, which descends about seven miles to Eureka Creek just south of the peak. From there, pick a line up the south side or into the basin between Monument and Lake Mountain.

ways.name: Rainy Pass, the PCT north and the ridge above Porcupine Creek
ways.notes: Follow the PCT north from Rainy Pass about a mile and a half, to just before the Porcupine Creek bridge, then climb the ridge northeast for about two miles to the base. The shorter way, with the cleaner gully to the base.

ways.name: Cutthroat Lake and Cutthroat Pass
ways.notes: The eastern way: on trail most of the way, to Cutthroat Lake and up to Cutthroat Pass, then south along the crest for about a mile.

ways.name: Klahhane Ridge climbers' trail from Hurricane Ridge
ways.season: Mid-July to September
ways.notes: Paved path off the east end of the visitor centre lot, then open subalpine ridge for about two and a half miles to an unsigned split. A shorter, steeper start climbs from the Switchback Trail on the road below and joins higher up. Nothing dependable to drink past the visitor centre — carry it all.

ways.name: Switchback Trail up to Klahhane Ridge
ways.notes: A steep, short trail from the Hurricane Ridge Road up to the Klahhane Ridge trail, then the same climbers' path to the summit.

ways.name: Heather Park trail from Heart O' the Hills
ways.notes: The long way from low on the Hurricane Ridge Road: the Heather Park trail climbs around the west side of the peak to join the climbers' path.

name: Standard Scramble (Appleton Pass / Boulder Lake approach)

ways.name: Sol Duc River Trail to Appleton Pass
ways.season: Mid-July to September
ways.notes: Just under five miles upriver, crossing Crystal Creek on a suspension bridge, to the signed pass junction, then a couple of miles and roughly two thousand feet through forest and meadow to the gap. The Boulder Creek side reaches the same pass but is far longer now that the road below it is walked or ridden.

ways.name: Boulder Creek from the Elwha
ways.notes: From the Elwha side, follow the Boulder Creek trail past the old hot springs and climb to Appleton Pass, where it meets the Sol Duc line. It is the longer way, since the road below the trailhead may have to be walked or biked. Boulder Lake makes a good side camp.

ways.name: Bailey Range crest to Bear Pass
ways.season: Late July to mid-September
ways.notes: This peak has two genuinely different journeys to it: the western one from the Sol Duc over the High Divide and along the Bailey crest through Cat Basin, Ferry Basin and Stephen Peak, and the eastern one up the Elwha with a long road walk or ride added at the start. Both take days. Almost every ascent is a side-summit off a traverse rather than a trip in its own right.

ways.name: Up the Elwha to Elwha Basin
ways.notes: The eastern way: follow the Elwha River trail up the full length of the valley past Hayes River and Chicago Camp to Elwha Basin, then climb onto the peak from the basin. It takes several days, and a road walk or bike ride may be needed to reach the trailhead.

ways.name: Kindy Ridge from the Kindy Creek road
ways.notes: Up Kindy Ridge from the Kindy Creek road off the Cascade River Road, then south through the Buckindy high country to below the north side. A longer two-to-three-day approach.

ways.name: Green Mountain trail and the Horse Lake saddle
ways.notes: The usual way: up the Green Mountain trail off the Suiattle River Road, then cross-country east and southeast along the ridges past Misch to Buckindy's north side. Check the Suiattle River Road before you go; it has been closed to vehicles for long stretches.

ways.name: The south gully below the Carru-Lago col
ways.season: Mid-July to September
ways.notes: Carru sits between Osceola and the higher Mount Lago and is almost always climbed as one summit of several on a multi-day trip out of the Harts Pass road end. Two lines reach the country below it: the shorter drops from Slate Pass and Buckskin Ridge into the Middle Fork Pasayten, then goes by Fred's Lake and over the ridge crest into upper Eureka Creek and Shellrock Basin; the Monument Creek trail is longer with more up and down. Tread through this wilderness is lightly maintained, with blowdown on the valley trail and stretches where the path is fainter on the ground than it looks on a map. The climb itself is short, well under two hours from the base, and unremarkable, essentially a heap of scree and talus with parallel ribs running up it.

ways.name: From Slate Pass down the Middle Fork Pasayten
ways.notes: The shorter and more common start. From Slate Pass the trail drops north to the Middle Fork Pasayten; follow it up-valley past the Berk Creek junction, then climb toward Fred's Lake and Shellrock Basin below Carru. Most parties combine Carru with Osceola and Lago over two or three days.

ways.name: Phelps Creek and Leroy Basin, over the col and across the Gloomy Glacier
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the Leroy-to-Gloomy crossing runs through avalanche terrain earlier than that
ways.notes:
Same walk in as for Seven Fingered Jack and Maude: Phelps Creek trail to the Leroy Creek crossing at about 4,140 ft, then the steep unmaintained climbers' trail on the north side of the creek into Leroy Basin at about 6,100 ft.

This is the common approach but not the elegant one. It exists because the alternative is the ferry up Lake Chelan to Holden and the Railroad Creek trail into Copper Basin, which gains the East Ridge — the standard route — much more directly. A third option starts at Cottonwood on the Entiat River and reaches the East Ridge by way of the Entiat Glacier. All three converge on the same south-east face finish.

From Leroy Basin, head north-west toward a waterfall and climb its left side to a small notch on the ridge of Seven Fingered Jack. Published descriptions of this saddle vary — one places it just west of an obvious 7,700 ft col with a couple of bivy sites at the low point, another gives it as a notch reached past a second creek crossing — and they may or may not be the same feature, so check it on a map rather than assuming.

From the saddle you must drop about a thousand feet into the moraine at the terminus of the Gloomy Glacier, and every foot of it has to be regained on the way out. Two published ways down: descend to the tarn below and go around a prominent rock formation that guards the basin, or descend to the right across sandy ledges and down large boulders.

Expect roughly nine hours round trip from Leroy Basin, and a very long day car to car — one party left the trailhead at three in the morning and got back at eleven at night.

ways.name: Holden Village and Copper Basin
ways.notes: From Holden Village up to the Copper–Entiat divide and the east ridge. The most direct way to the standard east-side line, and climbable in a day from Holden, but it depends on the Lake Chelan boat.

ways.name: Entiat River from Cottonwood
ways.notes: Up the Entiat River trail toward the Entiat Glacier and the east ridge. The longest way in, with less gain and little avalanche exposure.

ways.name: First Divide from the Duckabush and Marmot Lake
ways.season: Mid-July to September
ways.notes: The historic Skokomish approach is closed by fire damage, and so is this one where it leaves the Duckabush: the park lists the Home Sweet Home Trail, from the Duckabush River Trail junction over First Divide, closed for the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire with no reopening date (trail-conditions page updated September 14, 2026), so no open trail reaches First Divide while the closure stands. When it reopens, the way in is the long Duckabush valley over Big Hump to Marmot Lake, then back to the Home Sweet Home junction and over First Divide. Roughly double the old distance and firmly a multi-day trip with a camp at the lake or at Home Sweet Home.

ways.name: Staircase and the North Fork Skokomish to First Divide
ways.notes: The historic and shortest way in. From Staircase, follow the North Fork Skokomish trail up the valley to Home Sweet Home and on to First Divide, where the scramble leaves the trail. Fire damage has affected this corridor, so check the park's trail status before planning.

ways.name: From Robinson Creek over Robinson Pass
ways.season: Mid-July to September
ways.notes: Lago is the highest peak in this group and the least loved underfoot, being a large pile of loose rock where the whole ascent asks for deliberate movement rather than any technique. Camp is normally Fred's Lake or Shellrock Basin, reached along the Middle Fork Pasayten, either over Robinson Pass from the low Robinson Creek trailhead or down the Whistler Cutoff from the high start at Slate Pass, with an awkward crossing of upper Eureka Creek when it is swollen with snowmelt. From camp the round trip is a half day. Many parties link straight over to Carru by the connecting col rather than descending and re-climbing, and the southwest slope is a common variation for coming down since it avoids some of the steeper upper rock ribs.

ways.name: From Slate Pass down the Middle Fork Pasayten
ways.notes: The high start most parties use. From Slate Pass the trail drops north into the Middle Fork Pasayten; follow it down-valley past the Berk Creek junction, then climb to Fred's Lake or Shellrock Basin to camp. Lago is usually combined with Carru and Osceola.

ways.name: Park Creek Pass and the heather traverse to the Fremont saddle and the hogsback
ways.season: July and August
ways.notes:
The standard start is the Colonial Creek Campground trailhead on SR-20 near milepost 130, about 1,060-1,200 ft, and the Thunder Creek trail south for roughly 16-18 miles to the Thunder Basin camp area around 6,000 ft and on to Park Creek Pass. A southern alternative reaches the same pass from Stehekin: the High Bridge guard station near 1,600 ft, the Stehekin River trail to the Park Creek trailhead, then the Park Creek trail past Buckner Camp — with a creek crossing on a less-than-substantial footlog that is genuinely nerve-wracking in the dark.

From Park Creek Pass leave the maintained trail and traverse gradually northward around a broad ridge through open heather and high alpine terrain, roughly a mile and a half to two miles, crossing a rib around 7,600 ft and a steep gully through cliff bands around 7,350 ft that can hold snow or ice. That brings you to the Fremont Glacier saddle around 8,000-8,250 ft, where rock-outcrop bivy sites with nearby running water make the standard high camp.

From camp it is about three and a half hours to the summit.

ways.name: Stehekin and the Park Creek trail to Park Creek Pass
ways.notes: From the Park Creek Trailhead on the Stehekin Valley Road, the Park Creek trail climbs to Park Creek Pass and joins the Thunder Creek line there. It needs the Lake Chelan boat and the Stehekin shuttle to reach the trailhead.

ways.name: Easy Pass and Fisher Basin
ways.season: July to September; the Easy Pass trail usually holds snow until July
ways.notes:
The usual way in while SR 20 is open. From the Easy Pass Trailhead near milepost 151, climb about 3.5 miles to the 6,500-ft pass, drop into Fisher Basin, and follow the Fisher Creek Trail down the valley — past a good log bridge with a handrail — to the stream that drains the lake camp near 5,160 ft below the Banded Glacier. About ten miles one way. The trailhead sits inside the highway's winter closure, and the pass is often snowbound until July.

From the lake camp, climb south-southeast to a low point on the ridge, sometimes called Christmas Tree Col, which may need a rope for steep snow or a short glacier section. Drop onto the Banded Glacier on the far side and ascend it to the Banded-Douglas Col.

The last two thirds of this route is sustained off-trail goat-path route-finding, and the scree below the glacier is described as moving like a Newtonian fluid: much easier to ascend than to descend. Party size in this NPS zone is capped at six.

ways.name: Thunder Creek and Fisher Creek
ways.season: Whenever SR 20 is closed at Easy Pass, or in the shoulder season
ways.notes:
The longer way in, and the one that stays open all year: the Colonial Creek trailhead is west of SR 20's winter closure gates. Take the Thunder Creek Trail from Colonial Creek Campground near 1,200 ft about nine miles to the Fisher Creek Trail junction, then the Fisher Creek Trail about three miles, past the handrailed log bridge, to the stream that drains the lake camp near 5,160 ft. Roughly thirteen miles one way, with Neve Camp under two miles in for a late start.

From the lake camp, climb south-southeast to a low point on the ridge, sometimes called Christmas Tree Col, which may need a rope for steep snow or a short glacier section. Drop onto the Banded Glacier on the far side and ascend it to the Banded-Douglas Col.

The last two thirds of this route is sustained off-trail goat-path route-finding, and the scree below the glacier is described as moving like a Newtonian fluid: much easier to ascend than to descend. Party size in this NPS zone is capped at six.

ways.name: Low Divide and Seattle Basin to the Noyes–Meany col
ways.season: Late July to mid-September
ways.notes: Low Divide is reached up the North Fork Quinault, or from the Elwha with a long road walk or ride added at the start. Almost nobody comes for this peak alone — it is normally tagged while linking Christie, Meany and Seattle from one camp near the divide or in Seattle Basin.

ways.name: Elwha River to Low Divide
ways.notes: The Elwha trail about 28 miles to Low Divide, plus the closed road walk at each end. Much longer, and used for traverses from the north.

ways.name: Depot Creek from the Canadian side
ways.notes: The unmaintained Depot Creek trail crosses the border to Ouzel Lake, then the bench leads east to the south side. The easiest and most used way, but it means crossing the border on foot away from a port of entry, so confirm the entry rules first, and the road needs high clearance.

ways.name: Silver Creek from Ross Lake
ways.notes: The all-US way: a water taxi up Ross Lake to the mouth of Silver Creek, then a long bushwhack up Silver Creek to Silver Lake and north to the upper terrace. Harder and much brushier.

ways.name: Paradise and Glacier Vista, across the Nisqually to the Turtle and Camp Hazard
ways.season: Roughly mid-May to early Aug; the ice holds into summer but the approach and glacier conditions degrade quickly after the start of August
ways.notes:
From Paradise at 5,400 ft, the common approach follows the Skyline Trail to Glacier Vista and the Nisqually Moraine, then drops west onto the glacier. The route crosses the lower Nisqually, gains the Wilson Glacier and climbs to the Turtle Snowfield, with camps at The Castle around 9,200-9,500 ft and Camp Hazard at 10,800 ft at the top of the snowfield.

Roped travel and crevasse-rescue readiness are needed from the moment you leave the Nisqually. Water is available from snowmelt lower down on the Comet Falls and Van Trump side but not once you are on glacier ice.

Rockfall and icefall off the Wapowety Cleaver and the Kautz Icefall are the approach-zone hazards; move through the exposed ground early and efficiently.

ways.name: Comet Falls and Van Trump Park
ways.notes: Climbs from the Comet Falls trailhead past Van Trump Park and up the moraine beside the remnant Van Trump Glacier, joining the Paradise line around the Castle and the base of the Turtle. Preferred late in the season: it never crosses the Nisqually and has running water low down, but it starts about 1,700 ft lower and the descent is easy to lose in the trees.

ways.name: Low Divide and Seattle Meadows
ways.season: Late July to mid-September
ways.notes: Reached up the North Fork Quinault or by the higher, rougher Skyline Ridge primitive route past Three Lakes and Kimta Peak, or from the Elwha side. Two other lines come in through Noyes Basin and directly up Seattle Creek Basin. Whichever you pick, plan on a multi-day backpack just to reach a base camp.

ways.name: Up the Elwha to Low Divide
ways.notes: The long northern way: follow the Elwha River trail up the whole valley past Hayes River and Chicago Camp, then climb to Low Divide. It takes several days, and a road walk or bike ride may be needed to reach the trailhead.

ways.name: Mount Townsend Trail #839 from the Upper Trailhead
ways.season: Late June to October
ways.notes: Three sets of switchbacks, the last fully sun-exposed and the hottest, most water-hungry part of the day — there is no dependable creek on the trail itself. Camp Windy and an unmarked spur to Windy Lake sit at about 5,300 ft. The Lower Trailhead adds roughly two round-trip miles and five hundred feet. The small upper lot fills early on summer weekends.

ways.name: Little Quilcene Trail over Little River Summit
ways.notes: The shortest way to the top, with the least gain. The trail climbs steadily through forest to Little River Summit, then follows an open, exposed ridge for the last mile to meet the main trail near the summit. Carry water, as the ridge is dry and sunny.

ways.name: Goat Pass and the Stuart Glacier to the fourth-class gully and the notch
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; earlier the gully to the notch holds snow and the glacier crossing is simpler, later it is bare and looser
ways.notes:
From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road, take the Ingalls Way trail over Ingalls Pass, past Ingalls Lake toward Stuart Pass, then the climbers' path onto the talus shoulder under Stuart's West Ridge and northwest to Goat Pass at about 7,600 ft.

From Goat Pass, traverse onto and across the Stuart Glacier rather than along beneath it, aiming for a fourth-class gully that runs up to the obvious notch in the North Ridge. This is the difference between this route and the complete ridge in one sentence: the complete-ridge party traverses east below the glacier to the toe, this party crosses the glacier and goes up.

The notch is a bivy: there are two good sites in it, which is why parties who intend to climb the upper ridge in a day from a high camp use it.

Published descriptions of this route are frank that the last of the navigation is yours — one of them says outright to take a topographic map and work it out. Treat that as a real warning rather than as rhetoric.

ways.name: Mountaineer Creek and the Stuart Glacier from the north
ways.notes: From the Stuart Lake trailhead, follow the trail up Mountaineer Creek, then leave it for the climbers' path into the basin below the Stuart and Sherpa glaciers. Climb the Stuart Glacier to the notch where the upper ridge begins. This suits parties camping in the north-side basin, but leaves the car on the opposite side from the Cascadian Couloir descent.

ways.name: Lyman Lakes basin to the south flank
ways.season: Late July to September; axe early
ways.notes: Access is the hard part and it has changed. The classic way in is by passenger ferry up Lake Chelan and a village shuttle to the Railroad Creek trail, then a long valley walk to the Lyman Lakes basin — but that corridor has been shut by flood and landslide damage with no near-term reopening, so plan instead on the longer route in from the Phelps Creek side over Spider Gap, which is eleven or twelve miles one way and involves glacier travel with an axe. Either way this is a camp-in-the-basin objective, not a day out. Maintained tread effectively ends at the lakes; everything above is picked by eye with no path and no cairns. It is commonly paired with the lower summit less than a mile to its south from the same camp.

ways.name: Phelps Creek over Spider Gap
ways.notes: The Phelps Creek trail to Spider Meadow, over Spider Gap and down to Lyman Lakes, then the same basin to the south flank. No boat needed.

ways.name: North Fork Entiat over Saska Pass and Snow Brushy Creek
ways.season: Mid-July to September; axe early
ways.notes: A long, largely off-trail approach through burned country for a summit that is barely a scramble. From the North Fork Entiat road end the tread runs up-valley past the Fern Lake spur to the Pyramid Mountain junction, which is the usual last camp with water; fill there, because the drainages between it and the pass are seasonal and often dry. Gain Saska Pass by climbing the drainage directly rather than following the sidehill traverse, which is slower and more tiring across scree. From the pass you lose about 1,500 ft into the Snow Brushy burn, where the tread is gone entirely and ash-covered slopes and fallen snags erase any line, then regain nineteen hundred feet or so out of the creek — that descent and reclimb are what make the day long, not the peak. A separate approach exists up the Entiat River trail and the sheep driveway from the south, also through heavy fire blowdown.

ways.name: Entiat River trail and Snow Brushy Creek to Borealis Pass
ways.notes: From the Entiat River trailhead just past Cottonwood Campground, walk the Entiat River trail about six and a half miles to the Snow Brushy Creek trail, then follow it up-valley about five miles; the creek crossing there is a reliable place for water. A faint, sometimes hard-to-follow trail branches north and climbs to Borealis Pass in about a mile, below the easy south slopes of the peak. Much of the valley is burned, so expect downed timber.

ways.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core, then a hundred feet right of the left-flank classic
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
ways.notes:
The shared Core Enchantments approach: Stuart Lake trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail to the Colchuck Lake Trail junction, across Mountaineer Creek and up to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, then the boulder field at the south end and Aasgard Pass — 2,000 ft in 1.25 miles of loose scree, the crux of the walk in, dangerous under snow into early July and avalanche-prone in shoulder season.

From the pass, cross-country north past Isolation and Tranquil Lake toward Gnome Tarn and the base of the south face — roughly 7.5 to 8 miles and 4,600 ft one way, the last stretch unmarked over slabs and talus.

Four pitches, about 450 ft: a short crack and slab to a corner, a long exposed and somewhat dirty face-crack pitch, a corner with a bouldery move, and a finishing fingers-to-hands pitch to the ridge.

ways.name: Snow Lakes and the lower Enchantments
ways.notes: The longer, more gradual way in from Icicle Creek Road: the Snow Lakes trail climbs past Nada and Snow lakes to Lake Vivianne, about ten miles with well over 5,000 ft of gain, looking straight at Prusik's south face. From Vivianne continue past the upper lakes to the base of the face below Prusik Pass. It avoids the loose grind of Aasgard Pass at the cost of roughly two more miles and a thousand more feet.

ways.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core, to the left side of the south face
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
ways.notes:
The shared Core Enchantments approach: Stuart Lake trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail to the Colchuck Lake Trail junction, across Mountaineer Creek to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, the boulder field at the south end, and Aasgard Pass — 2,000 ft of loose scree in 1.25 miles, hazardous under snow into early July.

From the pass, cross-country north past Isolation and Tranquil Lake toward Gnome Tarn, roughly 7.5 to 8 miles and 4,600 ft one way from the trailhead.

Five pitches, about 450 ft: a burly and somewhat dirty roof pitch straight off the deck, an exposed corner to a good ledge, a short aid section through steep ground, a fingery crack between two features, and then the final corner crack shared with the neighbouring line to finish.

Because it joins that neighbour near the top, it shares its descent: a single full-length rappel on the north side and about thirty minutes of scrambling back round to the base.

ways.name: Snow Lakes and the lower Enchantments
ways.notes: The longer, more gradual way in from Icicle Creek Road: the Snow Lakes trail climbs past Nada and Snow lakes to Lake Vivianne, about ten miles with well over 5,000 ft of gain, looking straight at Prusik's south face. From Vivianne continue past the upper lakes to Prusik Pass and round onto the west face. It avoids the loose grind of Aasgard Pass at the cost of roughly two more miles and a thousand more feet.

ways.name: The far end of the Eldorado ice cap: five glaciers and a notch at the McAllister-Klawatti col
ways.season: Mid-July through August, when the glacier bridges are most consolidated and whiteout risk is lowest
ways.notes:
This is the way to Primus's south side, and it comes from the opposite side of the mountain to the Thunder Creek approach. From the Eldorado Creek trailhead on Cascade River Road near 2,100 ft, cross the North Fork Cascade River, climb the steep root-laced boot path through timber, cross the boulder field around 4,000 ft following cairns on the right side of the talus, and reach the meadows of Eldorado Basin. Continue to the toe of the Eldorado Glacier and rope up — it is broken and thinly bridged in a normal-to-low snow year.

From the upper Eldorado Glacier, traverse north below Eldorado's east ridge and continue on the Inspiration Glacier toward Klawatti Col near 7,800 ft. Parties describe crossing the Inspiration's crevasse fields with zero visibility, so plan for it.

Summit day from a Klawatti Col camp: downclimb or make a short rappel of about 50 ft through the notch at the McAllister-Klawatti col onto the Klawatti Glacier, rope up, and traverse below the south side of Austera's east ridge, rounding its end near 6,800 ft onto the North Klawatti Glacier — probing, because this stretch has caught parties by surprise even in good visibility — to the foot of Primus's south side. Then unrope and walk.

The route crosses the Eldorado, Inspiration, McAllister, Klawatti and North Klawatti glaciers in sequence; Austera Towers is passed and bypassed on a short scree ramp along the glacier's eastern edge.

ways.name: Thunder Creek and the Borealis Glacier: the east ridge from Lucky Pass
ways.notes:
The other way onto Primus comes from the north, and it finishes on a different line: the east ridge, not this route's south side. From Colonial Creek Campground on the North Cascades Highway, walk the Thunder Creek Trail about six miles to McAllister Camp. The bridge over Thunder Creek there has washed out, so expect to ford cold, fast water or hunt for a log crossing.

Across the creek, a faint, steep boot path climbs the long, brushy lower north ridge of Tricouni Peak to the toe of the Borealis Glacier near 6,000 ft, where there is good camping. From camp, climb the glacier along its eastern edge, keeping clear of the icefall in its middle, to Lucky Pass, the col between Primus and Tricouni near 7,200 ft, and follow the east ridge to the summit on class 3 ground.

The brush on the ridge above Thunder Creek is slow going in either direction, and worse carrying skis or a long pack.

ways.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core, fifty feet left of the standard south-face line
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the route is a hard rock climb and wants dry, warm granite
ways.notes:
The Core Enchantments approach: Stuart Lake trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail 2.5 miles to the Colchuck Lake Trail junction, across Mountaineer Creek and up the switchbacks to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft. From the boulder field at the lake's south end, Aasgard Pass — 1.25 miles gaining about 2,000 ft of steep loose scree and dirt, the physical crux of the approach, with a hidden creek and moat under lingering snow into early July.

From the pass at 7,841 ft, continue cross-country through the upper Core past Isolation and Tranquil Lake toward Prusik Pass and Gnome Tarn. Parties commonly bivy at the tarn, about twenty minutes from the base. There is no maintained trail for the last stretch.

The Snow Lakes trail is the longer alternative when Aasgard or the trailhead is closed: past Nada and Snow Lakes to Lake Viviane, then up and right toward Temple Lake and up climbers' paths through boulders to the base of the south face.

ways.name: Snow Lakes and the lower Enchantments
ways.notes: The longer, more gradual way in from Icicle Creek Road: the Snow Lakes trail climbs past Nada and Snow lakes to Lake Vivianne, about ten miles with well over 5,000 ft of gain, looking straight at Prusik's south face. From Vivianne continue past the upper lakes to the base of the south face. It avoids the loose grind of Aasgard Pass at the cost of roughly two more miles and a thousand more feet.

ways.name: Colchuck Lake and Aasgard Pass
ways.notes: The usual way in. From the Stuart Lake trailhead walk the Colchuck Lake trail to Colchuck Lake, then climb the loose boulders and scree of Aasgard Pass into the Core Enchantments. Walk down through the basin past Perfection Lake toward Prusik Pass and scramble up to the base of the south face; Aasgard is steep and can hold snow into early summer.

ways.name: Snow Lakes and the lower Enchantments
ways.notes: The longer, more gradual way in from Icicle Creek Road: the Snow Lakes trail climbs past Nada and Snow lakes to Lake Vivianne, about ten miles with well over 5,000 ft of gain, looking straight at Prusik's south face. From Vivianne continue past the upper lakes to the base of the south face. It avoids the loose grind of Aasgard Pass at the cost of roughly two more miles and a thousand more feet.

ways.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core to the left flank of the south face
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
ways.notes:
As for the rest of the face: Stuart Lake trailhead at about 3,400 ft, Stuart Lake Trail two and a half miles to the signed Colchuck Lake Trail junction, left and across Mountaineer Creek — a rock-hop or log crossing, and the last easy water for a while — then 1.6 miles of switchbacks to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft.

Boulder-hop the east shore to the boulder field at the south end, then Aasgard Pass: 2,000 ft in 1.25 miles of steep loose dirt and scree, cairned when snow-free. In early season, and often into July, snow bridges a hidden creek and moat on the left side of the gully; people have been badly hurt and killed there postholing or glissading into it.

From the pass at 7,841 ft, drop into the upper Core past Isolation and Tranquil Lake and continue cross-country a mile or so north over slabs and heather benches toward Prusik Pass and Gnome Tarn. The start is fifteen to twenty minutes from a Gnome Tarn camp.

ways.name: Snow Lakes and the lower Enchantments
ways.notes: The longer, more gradual way in from Icicle Creek Road: the Snow Lakes trail climbs past Nada and Snow lakes to Lake Vivianne, about ten miles with well over 5,000 ft of gain, looking straight at Prusik's south face. From Vivianne continue past the upper lakes to the base of the south face. It avoids the loose grind of Aasgard Pass at the cost of roughly two more miles and a thousand more feet.

ways.name: Aasgard Pass to Gnome Tarn
ways.season: Jul-Sep; earlier the pass is a snow climb and the Core travel is on snow
ways.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead, Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A across Mountaineer Creek and up the switchbacks to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft — about four miles and 2,000-2,200 ft.

From the boulder field at the lake's south end, climb Aasgard Pass: roughly 2,000 ft in a little over a mile of loose scree and dirt, and the crux of the day. Stay climber's left of the cliff bands; the terrain to climber's right, toward the waterfalls on Colchuck Peak's flank, cliffs out and has killed people. Snow lingering into early July hides a creek running beneath the talus.

From the pass at 7,841 ft travel cross-country through the Core, dropping from Talisman Lake toward Rune Lake, then ascending to the gentle ridge east of Rune's upper basin to reach Gnome Tarn. Gnome Tarn is the standard camp for this face and sits close under it.

A longer approach on the Snow Lakes Trail exists and is the fallback when Aasgard or the Stuart Lake trailhead is closed; some parties deliberately go in over Aasgard and out via Snow Lakes, about 21 miles, to spare their knees a second descent of the pass.

The last stretch to the wall is unmarked cross-country over slabs and talus.

ways.name: Snow Lakes and the lower Enchantments
ways.notes: The longer, more gradual way in from Icicle Creek Road: the Snow Lakes trail climbs past Nada and Snow lakes to Lake Vivianne, about ten miles with well over 5,000 ft of gain, looking straight at Prusik's south face. From Vivianne continue past the upper lakes to Gnome Tarn and the base of the south face. It avoids the loose grind of Aasgard Pass at the cost of roughly two more miles and a thousand more feet.

ways.name: Shellrock Pass camp and the south side
ways.season: Mid-July to September
ways.notes: Ptarmigan is one of the most isolated summits in this wilderness, sitting less than a mile from the most remote point in it, and the whole difficulty is getting underneath it. From the Slate Pass road end the standard line drops through larch and avalanche-lily meadows to the Middle Fork Pasayten trail, runs down-valley through a stretch with a long-standing reputation for blowdown, then climbs by Fred's Lake and over the pass at the head of Eureka Creek to Shellrock Pass. A broad bench just southwest of the pass is the standard high camp for this peak and its neighbours. From the south the mountain is a rounded, tundra-covered massif and the walking is genuinely easy; its north side is another matter entirely.

ways.name: Eightmile Creek, Eightmile Pass and the Hidden Lakes
ways.notes: The shortest line on the map, but it starts below 3,500 ft instead of high on the Slate Pass road. From the trailhead at the end of Eightmile Creek Road, cross Eightmile Pass and follow the trail past the Hidden Lakes to Ptarmigan Creek, northeast of the peak, then go a further two or three miles to the base. Expect a long day of trail before any climbing.

ways.name: Andrews Creek to Remmel Lake
ways.notes: The shortest line to the peak. Walk the Andrews Creek trail up the valley past the Meadow Lake and Peepsight junctions, then continue to Remmel Lake at the foot of the northwest ridge. The lower valley is burned and can hold a lot of blowdown.

ways.name: Chewuch River trail to Remmel Lake
ways.notes: A longer but gentler and generally better-kept trail. From the Thirtymile trailhead at the end of the Chewuch road, follow the Chewuch River trail north toward Four Point Lake and on to Remmel Lake. Most parties break the walk with a night along the river.

ways.name: Reynolds Creek Trail and the South Fork drainage
ways.season: Mid-July to September; axe for snow
ways.notes: The short way in, and short is relative. From the road end off the Twisp River an unmaintained primitive trail climbs through forest alongside the creek for roughly three miles. Above the confluence the tread gives out and about two miles of intermittent bushwhacking through slide alder, downed timber and a boot path that comes and goes is the real crux of the day — several parties lose more time here than on the mountain. The basin above holds snow well into summer, so an axe is worth carrying even when the valley looks dry. A longer alternative comes in over War Creek Ridge from the Williams Creek side and can be strung into a loop with a neighbouring summit, but it joins the same finish. Mark the point where you leave the tread; it is easy to miss coming down.

ways.name: Williams Lake and War Creek Ridge
ways.notes: Longer, but on good trail at first and far more scenic. From the Williams Creek trailhead on the West Twisp River road at about 2,800 ft, follow the well-marked trail to Williams Lake at about 6,500 ft, then climb over Williams Butte and follow War Creek Ridge toward Camel's Hump. Drop through a boulder break in the cliffs into the upper South Fork Reynolds Creek basin and climb heather and scree to the summit pyramid.

ways.name: Le Conte-Sentinel col from Yang Yang Lakes
ways.season: Late July to mid-September, and climbed in the morning — the basin snow takes crampons cleanly at dawn and goes soft by afternoon
ways.notes: This peak is reached from a camp on the Ptarmigan Traverse rather than from a road end. From Cascade Pass go over Cache Col to Kool-Aid Lake, take the Red Ledge beneath Art's Knoll through the cliff band, cross to Yang Yang Lakes, then climb the broad Le Conte Glacier to the notch north of the peak. The notch carries dry bivy platforms and most parties leave overnight gear there and climb on light packs.

ways.name: Downey Creek and the south end of the traverse
ways.notes: From the Downey Creek trailhead on the Suiattle River Road, walk the Downey Creek trail and the brushy Bachelor Creek path to Cub Lake and Itswoot Ridge, then cross the Dana Glacier country to White Rock Lakes. From the lakes, work back up onto the South Cascade Glacier to reach the peak. Plan on several days of off-trail and glacier travel.

ways.name: The shared Goode approach to 7,400 ft, then the talus cirque and the right-most notch
ways.season: Late July through September; snow often lingers in the basin above about 7,400 ft into early August, so carry an axe and consider crampons even for a nominally dry climb
ways.notes:
Storm King sits at the head of Thunder Creek and is one of the range's most remote summits — a three-day car-to-car trip is the norm, and three separate trailhead approaches converge on the same high basin below Goode's south side.

The most common is Thunder Creek: from Colonial Creek Campground on SR-20, the Thunder Creek trail roughly 13 miles with little gain to the McAllister Creek confluence, past Junction, Skagit Queen and Thunder Basin camps, then the Park Creek Pass trail junction and the switchbacks to Park Creek Pass. Alternatives are McAlester Pass and Rainbow Creek from SR-20, or a boat or shuttle to Stehekin and High Bridge Camp then the Park Creek trail from the south. From Stehekin the boot path starts on the north side of a large whitish-rock washout about two miles above the Two Mile camp, near 4,100 ft, five minutes further into the woods.

Every approach joins that trail: from Thunder Creek, cross Park Creek Pass and descend its south side to the washout. Leave the trail at the small cairn, climb the burned ridge beside the washout ravine, trend climber's left through heather and game trails, and follow cairns above about 6,500 ft to the basin below Goode at about 7,400 ft. From there, traverse snow and talus, favouring climber's left, roughly a mile to the cirque below Storm King's east and west towers. A rib camp around 7,450 ft with nearby water is the usual base.

From the cirque, a long and very loose talus and scree slope leads up toward the southwest gully system. Helmet on and space out — that slope is the approach's main hazard.

ways.name: Stehekin and the Park Creek trail
ways.notes: Take the boat up the lake to Stehekin and the shuttle to High Bridge, then walk up the valley past Bridge Creek to the Park Creek trail and climb it past Two Mile Camp. About a mile before Five Mile Camp, look for cairns marking a class 2-3 climbers' path up to the basin below Goode at about 7,400 ft. The least climbing of the three ways if the boat and shuttle schedule suits.

ways.name: Cascade Pass and the upper Stehekin valley
ways.notes: A drive-to start from the west side when the boat is impractical. Cross Cascade Pass and descend into the Stehekin valley, follow it down to the Park Creek trail, then climb Park Creek to the same cairned climbers' path up to the basin below Goode.

ways.name: Foggy Dew Creek and Merchants Basin to Cooney Lake
ways.season: Mid-July to early October; larch Sep
ways.notes: Most parties backpack in and camp at one of the lakes rather than push the whole eighteen to twenty mile round trip in a day. From the Foggy Dew road end the trail climbs the North Fork past a two-tiered cascade — the last easy water before the country opens — and tops out of the timber into a wildflower basin below the ridge, where a spur trail branches toward the lake. An alternative comes in on the Crater Creek and Eagle Lake trail, taking a signed cutoff south past a second set of lakes to reach the same lake basin. Above the lake the ground is dry, so fill there. Larches turn gold around the basin in late September, which is a fine but colder window with a real chance of early snow icing the summit blocks.

ways.name: Crater Creek and the Eagle Lakes side
ways.notes: A higher start at about 4,760 ft and a gentler grade, with a creek ford. From the Crater Creek trailhead follow the Eagle Lakes trail a little over two miles, then the Martin Creek trail to the Cooney Lake trail; parties can also base at Upper Eagle Lake and cross Horsehead Pass. Often used to make a loop with the Foggy Dew side.

ways.name: Surprise Creek past Surprise and Glacier lakes
ways.notes: The more popular way in, from a trailhead that is easy to find near Scenic on US 2. Climb the Surprise Creek trail to Surprise Lake, join the Pacific Crest Trail and follow it north to Trap Pass, then take the unofficial path south from the pass to the Thunder Mountain lakes basin under the north face.

ways.name: Tunnel Creek, Hope Lake and the PCT
ways.notes: From the Tunnel Creek trailhead off US 2, climb about a mile and a half to Hope Lake on the Pacific Crest Trail. Follow the PCT south a couple of miles over meadowy ground and up the switchbacks to Trap Pass, then take the unofficial path south to the Thunder Mountain lakes basin.

ways.name: Trail 342 from Long Swamp
ways.season: Late June to early October
ways.notes: This is the easternmost of the high peaks here and by far the least technical, being a trail walk with a very short scramble stapled on the end, so the real work is the drive. Long gravel forest roads out of Loomis reach Long Swamp Campground, where Trail 342 starts and climbs steadily through burned lodgepole and recovering meadow to a camp with water partway up and then out onto open, treeless ridge. A shorter trail comes in from the Cathedral Driveway trailhead a few miles further west but is overgrown in stretches from lack of use, and a third start at Iron Gate involves the roughest driving of the three. Water on the upper trail is limited and seasonal, so carry enough for a long day.

ways.name: Windy Creek trail from Cathedral Driveway
ways.notes: The shortest way up. From the Cathedral Driveway trailhead, a few miles west of Long Swamp on the same road, climb the Windy Creek trail about five miles to its junction with the Windy Peak trail, then go a short distance more to the summit. Some maps wrongly show the trail starting from the Cathedral Driveway trail about half a mile west of the trailhead.

ways.name: Boundary Trail from Iron Gate
ways.notes: The roughest drive of the three. From FR-39, turn onto FR-3900-500 and follow it about six miles to the Iron Gate trailhead; a high-clearance vehicle is recommended and passenger cars are not advised. Hike north on the Boundary Trail toward Sunny Pass and Horseshoe Basin, then take the Windy Peak trail west to the summit scramble.
